sportboot-binnen-elwis-237.question: How must a vessel operator behave during flood/high water?

options.a: Adjust speed and stay as far as possible in the middle of the fairway; if applicable, observe special speed limits and navigation restrictions.
options.b: Adjust speed and stay as far as possible in the middle of the fairway; special speed limits and navigation restrictions do not need to be observed.
options.c: Adjust speed and stay as far as possible on the right side in the direction of travel; if applicable, observe special speed limits and navigation restrictions.
options.d: Adjust speed and stay as far as possible on the left side in the direction of travel; if applicable, observe special speed limits and navigation restrictions.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-237.explanation: During high water, current, water depth and the edges of the fairway change significantly; areas near the banks and shallow zones carry extra hazards from turbulence, floating debris and reduced clearance. The skipper must therefore adjust speed to the situation and keep as far as possible to the middle of the fairway to maintain a safe distance from both banks. In addition, waterway authorities frequently impose special speed limits and navigation restrictions during flood conditions, which must be observed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-7.question: What signal must a sailing vessel that counts as a power-driven vessel additionally show during the day?

options.a: A black cone, point down.
options.b: A black cone, point up.
options.c: Two black balls, one above the other.
options.d: A black diamond (rhombus).

sportboot-binnen-elwis-7.explanation: When a sailing vessel is also using its engine, it is legally classed as a power-driven vessel and must make this visible during the day as well, so other traffic can apply the correct right-of-way rules. The prescribed day shape for this is a black cone with its point down, shown clearly so it can be seen from all round.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-10.question: When must a vessel's lights be carried or shown?

options.a: From sunset to sunrise, and in reduced visibility.
options.b: From sunrise to sunset, and in reduced visibility.
options.c: In darkness, bad weather, and reduced visibility.
options.d: From 6:00 pm to 6:00 am, and in reduced visibility.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-10.explanation: Under the Inland Waterways Traffic Regulations, vessels must generally carry their prescribed lights throughout the entire period from sunset to sunrise, regardless of weather. In addition, the lights must also be shown during daytime periods of reduced visibility, such as fog, heavy rain or snow, since other vessels would otherwise be unable to make out the vessel's position and heading.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-11.question: What is the purpose of a vessel's navigation lights?

options.a: They show a vessel's course and speed.
options.b: They show a vessel's direction of travel and position.
options.c: They show a vessel's direction of travel and status/situation.
options.d: They show a vessel's direction of travel and course.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-11.explanation: The main purpose of navigation lights is to let other vessel operators recognize, in darkness or reduced visibility, both the heading (via masthead, side and stern lights) and the situation or status of a vessel, for example underway, stationary, under tow, or aground/disabled. Course and speed, by contrast, cannot be read from the lights alone.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-13.question: Which lights must a sailing vessel carry that is under way with both sail and engine power at the same time?

options.a: The lights prescribed for a sailing vessel.
options.b: The lights prescribed for a power-driven vessel.
options.c: Red and green sidelights and a red all-round light.
options.d: Two red all-round lights, one above the other.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-13.explanation: A sailing vessel that is simultaneously using its engine is legally classed as a power-driven vessel, even though its sails are set. It must therefore show the lights prescribed for power-driven vessels, with masthead light, sidelights and sternlight, rather than the simpler lighting configuration of a pure sailing vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-16.question: What does the following sound signal mean?

options.a: Towed convoy with restricted maneuverability, over 200 m in length.
options.b: General danger and warning signal.
options.c: Vessel at anchor, over 100 m in length.
options.d: 'Stay away' signal, clear the danger area immediately.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-16.explanation: The so-called 'stay away' signal is given mainly by large vessels, pushed convoys, or vessels with restricted maneuverability when, at blind spots such as tight bends, bridges or narrow stretches, they need the full width of the fairway and cannot give way themselves. It unambiguously orders all other vessels to clear the danger area immediately, since a collision would otherwise be imminent.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-30.question: What do these lights in front of a lock mean?

options.a: Lock in operation, wait for the exit signal according to the queue order.
options.b: Entry clear, lock gate is opening.
options.c: Entry clear, oncoming traffic is blocked.
options.d: Lock in operation, wait for the entry signal according to the queue order.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-30.explanation: Locks are fitted with a fixed light-signal system that regulates entering and leaving traffic, since the lock chamber can usually only be used in one direction at a time. The signal combination shown means that entry is permitted, while a corresponding signal on the other side keeps oncoming traffic blocked until the lockage is complete.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-82.question: What must a small craft's helmsman be able to do to steer safely?

options.a: Receive and give all information and instructions, perceive all sound signals, and have sufficient all-round visibility.
options.b: Perceive all sound signals and have sufficient all-round visibility.
options.c: Receive and give all information and instructions.
options.d: Receive and give all information and instructions, and have sufficient all-round visibility.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-82.explanation: For safe steering, the helmsman must be fully capable at all times: able to receive and pass on all information and instructions, to perceive all sound signals from other vessels in good time, and to have sufficient visibility all around in order to recognize dangerous situations early. If any one of these abilities is missing, safe steering cannot be guaranteed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-101.question: What signs mark obstacles such as groynes and stone dams on the right side of the waterway?

options.a: Poles with a top mark: green cone, point down, or a green-and-white striped float pole with a green cone.
options.b: Poles with a top mark: red cone, point down, or a red-and-white striped float pole with a red cylinder.
options.c: Poles with a top mark: green cone, point up, or a green-and-white striped float pole with a green cone.
options.d: Poles with a top mark: red cone, point up, or a red-and-white striped float pole with a red cylinder.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-101.explanation: To mark obstacles near the bank, such as groynes and stone dams, waterway authorities use a fixed colour scheme tied to the side of the waterway: obstacles on the right side are marked with red top marks, a red cone point-down on a pole, or a red-and-white striped floating pole with a red cylinder. This fixed colour-and-shape assignment lets the skipper reliably identify the location and side of the obstacle from a distance.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-102.question: What does a green-and-white striped float pole with a green cone point-up, or a green buoy with a green-and-white striped topmark and green cone point-up, mark?

options.a: Edge of the fairway on the left side of the waterway.
options.b: Obstacle on the right side of the waterway.
options.c: Edge of the fairway on the right side of the waterway.
options.d: Obstacle on the left side of the waterway.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-102.explanation: Unlike the red marks used for the right side, green top marks always indicate obstacles on the left side of the waterway. A green cone point-up on a green-and-white striped pole, or on a green buoy, therefore shows that there is an obstacle there, such as a groyne or stone dam, that must be avoided.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-104.question: What do two white lights, one above the other, on a stationary vessel mean?

options.a: A vessel at anchor whose anchor may endanger shipping.
options.b: A stationary pushed convoy.
options.c: A vessel over 135 m in length.
options.d: A vessel at anchor that has laid out two anchors.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-104.explanation: A stationary vessel normally shows only a single all-round white light on the side facing the fairway. Two white lights, one above the other, instead mark a vessel at anchor whose anchor and chain extend into the fairway area and could therefore endanger passing traffic; other vessels must keep correspondingly greater clearance.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-105.question: What light does a stationary vessel show?

options.a: A white masthead light and a white sternlight.
options.b: An all-round white light, visible from all sides, on the side facing the fairway.
options.c: The sidelights and a visible white all-round light.
options.d: An all-round white flashing light, visible from all sides, on the side facing the fairway.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-105.explanation: A stationary vessel, for example at anchor or made fast to the bank, must show a single all-round white light at night, visible from all directions, mounted on the side facing the fairway. This allows passing vessels to identify the stationary vessel as an obstacle from a great distance, regardless of the direction from which they approach.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-120.question: What do these lights mean?

options.a: Pushed convoy shorter than 110 m.
options.b: Pushed convoy longer than 110 m.
options.c: Vessel without mechanical propulsion, longer than 110 m.
options.d: Power-driven vessel longer than 110 m.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-120.explanation: Power-driven vessels over 110 m in length carry a second masthead light, positioned higher and further aft than the forward one, in addition to the normal masthead light. This second light source makes it recognisable at night that the vessel is unusually long, so other traffic can plan for correspondingly more room and greater safety clearance.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-121.question: What does this day shape mean?

options.a: Vessels with priority at a lock.
options.b: Towing vessel at the head of a towed convoy.
options.c: Vessel at anchor.
options.d: A vessel that is part of a towed convoy.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-121.explanation: A towed convoy consists of one or more towed vessels and the towing vessel at its head. So that other traffic can correctly judge the composition and overall length of the convoy, the towing vessel at the head shows its own defined day shape, distinguishing it from the towed vessels that follow.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-122.question: What does this day shape mean?

options.a: Towing vessel at the head of a towed convoy.
options.b: Vessel at anchor.
options.c: A vessel that is part of a towed convoy.
options.d: Vessels with priority at a lock.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-122.explanation: Vessels that are part of a towed convoy but are not the towing vessel at its head carry their own separate day shape. This lets oncoming traffic recognise that the vessel is a towed unit within a longer convoy, rather than a vessel navigating independently.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-123.question: What do these lights mean?

options.a: Pushed convoy under 110 m in length.
options.b: Pushed convoy underway, seen from ahead.
options.c: Pushed convoy underway, seen from astern.
options.d: Pushed convoy at anchor.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-123.explanation: A pushed convoy underway, seen from ahead, shows a characteristic arrangement of masthead lights that differs from the lighting of a single power-driven vessel. This distinctive lighting configuration signals from a distance that it is a composite unit, often very long and wide, for which other vessels need to allow extra room.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-124.question: What do these lights mean?

options.a: Freely navigating ferry.
options.b: Pushed convoy, seen from the starboard side.
options.c: Pushed convoy, seen from astern.
options.d: Ferry that is not freely navigating.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-124.explanation: Ferries that cannot navigate freely, for example cable ferries or reaction ferries running along a fixed guide, show their own lighting pattern, different from that of a freely navigating ferry. Other vessels need to recognise this because a non-free-navigating ferry is severely restricted in its freedom of movement and can barely give way itself.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-125.question: What do these lights mean?

options.a: Pushed convoy, seen from the starboard side.
options.b: Freely navigating ferry.
options.c: Ferry that is not freely navigating.
options.d: Pushed convoy, seen from astern.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-125.explanation: A freely navigating ferry, unlike a cable or reaction ferry, moves independently across the water without a fixed guide. It therefore shows its own combination of lights, distinguishing it both from a non-free-navigating ferry and from an ordinary power-driven vessel, so other vessels can recognise its particular right-of-way status in ferry traffic.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-127.question: What does this day shape mean?

options.a: Vessel carrying substances hazardous to health, distance when stationary 50 m.
options.b: Vessel carrying explosive substances, distance when stationary 100 m.
options.c: Vessel of the supervisory authorities on duty.
options.d: Vessel carrying flammable substances, distance when stationary 10 m.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-127.explanation: Vessels carrying dangerous goods must indicate this with blue cones as a day shape or blue lights as a night signal. A single blue cone or single blue light marks flammable substances and requires a minimum distance of 10 m to be kept from the vessel when it is stationary, in order to avoid fire and explosion hazards.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-128.question: What do two blue lights, one above the other, on a vessel mean?

options.a: Vessel carrying explosive substances, distance when stationary 100 m.
options.b: Vessel carrying flammable substances, distance when stationary 10 m.
options.c: Vessel of the supervisory authorities on duty.
options.d: Vessel carrying substances hazardous to health, distance when stationary 50 m.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-128.explanation: Two blue lights, one above the other, mark a vessel carrying substances hazardous to health, that is toxic substances. The number of blue cones or lights indicates the hazard class: one sign stands for flammable substances, two for substances hazardous to health, and three for explosive substances. With two signs, a minimum distance of 50 m must be kept when the vessel is stationary.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-129.question: What does this day shape mean?

options.a: Vessel carrying substances hazardous to health, distance when stationary 50 m.
options.b: Vessel of the supervisory authorities on duty.
options.c: Vessel carrying flammable substances, distance when stationary 10 m.
options.d: Vessel carrying explosive substances, distance when stationary 100 m.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-129.explanation: During the day too, the number of blue cones is used to mark the dangerous-goods class. Two blue cones correspond to two blue lights shown at night and stand for substances hazardous to health; a minimum distance of 50 m must be kept from this vessel when it is stationary.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-130.question: What do three blue lights, one above the other, on a vessel mean?

options.a: Vessel of the supervisory authorities on duty.
options.b: Vessel carrying explosive substances, distance when stationary 100 m.
options.c: Vessel carrying substances hazardous to health, distance when stationary 50 m.
options.d: Vessel carrying flammable substances, distance when stationary 10 m.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-130.explanation: Three blue lights, one above the other, represent the highest of the three hazard levels in this marking system: explosive substances. Because of the high risk involved, a particularly large minimum distance of 100 m must be kept from such a vessel when it is stationary.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-131.question: What does this day shape mean?

options.a: Vessel of the supervisory authorities on duty.
options.b: Vessel carrying flammable substances, distance when stationary 10 m.
options.c: Vessel carrying explosive substances, distance when stationary 100 m.
options.d: Vessel carrying substances hazardous to health, distance when stationary 50 m.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-131.explanation: As a day shape too, the highest marking level, three blue cones, corresponds to a cargo of explosive substances. Because of the explosion risk, the largest prescribed minimum distance of 100 m applies here when the vessel is stationary.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-134.question: A small sailing craft is underway at night on an inland waterway and shows a white all-round light at the masthead. What additional lights must be shown once the engine is started?

options.a: No further light needs to be shown.
options.b: A white flashing light must be shown.
options.c: A second white masthead light must be shown.
options.d: Sidelights immediately next to each other or in a single combined lantern.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-134.explanation: A small sailing craft may show simplified lights at night, including a white all-round light at the masthead. However, as soon as the engine is also started, the vessel becomes a power-driven vessel and must make this clear with additional sidelights, red and green, which may be shown immediately next to each other or in a single combined lantern.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-135.question: What lights must a small craft under engine power carry when it is towing another small craft without mechanical propulsion?

options.a: The lights of a small craft with mechanical propulsion.
options.b: The lights of a small craft with mechanical propulsion plus a second white masthead light.
options.c: Two white lights, one above the other.
options.d: A white all-round light.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-135.explanation: Simplified rules apply to small craft when towing: if a small craft under engine power tows another small craft without its own propulsion, the towing vessel only needs to show the normal lights of a power-driven small craft. The extra towing lights that larger vessels must show when towing are not required here.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-136.question: What lights must a towed small craft show?

options.a: The lights of a power-driven small craft.
options.b: A white all-round light.
options.c: A white flashing light.
options.d: Two white lights, one above the other.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-136.explanation: A towed small craft does not itself show vessel-type lights, since it is not navigating independently but is being pulled by another vessel. A single all-round white light, visible from all sides, is sufficient to keep it recognisable to other traffic as part of the tow.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-138.question: What are the prescribed arcs of visibility and colours of the lights carried on board?

options.a: Masthead light: white 135°, sternlight 225° white, sidelights: port red and starboard green, each 112.5°.
options.b: Masthead light: white 112.5°, sternlight 225° white, sidelights: port red and starboard green, each 112.5°.
options.c: Masthead light: white 225°, sternlight 112.5° white, sidelights: port red and starboard green, each 135°.
options.d: Masthead light: white 225°, sternlight 135° white, sidelights: port red and starboard green, each 112.5°.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-138.explanation: The arcs of visibility of the prescribed lights add up seamlessly to a full 360° all around: the masthead light, white, shines unbroken over 225°, from dead ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam on each side; the sternlight, white, covers the remaining 135° astern. The sidelights, red to port, green to starboard, each shine over 112.5°, from dead ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam on their own side, together covering exactly the same area as the masthead light.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-139.question: What light must a small craft without mechanical propulsion carry at minimum?

options.a: An all-round light visible from all sides, white.
options.b: Masthead and sternlight.
options.c: A tricolour lantern at the masthead.
options.d: Sidelights.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-139.explanation: A small craft without its own mechanical propulsion, for example a rowing boat or an unlit dinghy, must, at night, carry or be able to show in good time at least a white light visible from all sides, so that other vessels can perceive it at all and give way in time. A full lighting set with masthead, side and stern lights is not mandatory for such craft.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-143.question: Who must give way when a sailor with the wind on the port side meets a sailing yacht with the wind on the starboard side and showing a black cone, on a collision course?

options.a: Both sailing yachts, because one counts as a small craft with mechanical propulsion and the other has the wind on the port side.
options.b: The sailing yacht with wind on the port side, because it counts as a small sailing craft.
options.c: The sailing yacht with wind on the starboard side, because it counts as a small sailing craft.
options.d: The sailing yacht with wind on the starboard side, because it counts as a small craft with mechanical propulsion.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-143.explanation: When a sailing vessel additionally shows a black cone, it means the engine is also running and the vessel is legally classed as a power-driven vessel, regardless of which side the wind is on. The basic rule between a genuine sailing vessel and a motor-sailing vessel is that power-driven vessels must give way to sailing vessels; the more favourable wind side no longer matters for the motor-sailing vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-145.question: What do these lights mean?

options.a: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the starboard side. Avoid suction and wash.
options.b: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing not permitted.
options.c: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on either side. Avoid suction and wash.
options.d: Floating plant at work. Passing not permitted.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-145.explanation: Floating plant at work, for example a dredger or crane on the water, shows its own combination of lights, distinct from that of a wrecked or sunken vessel. When passing is permitted on either side, other vessels may pass on both sides but must reduce speed to avoid suction and wash, which could endanger the work site or the equipment.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-146.question: What do these day signals mean?

options.a: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on either side. Avoid suction and wash.
options.b: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing not permitted.
options.c: Floating plant at work. Passing not permitted.
options.d: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the starboard side. Avoid suction and wash.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-146.explanation: As a day shape too, the marking for floating plant at work differs from that of a wrecked vessel. When the shown combination of signs permits passage on either side, there is still an obligation to keep sufficient distance and avoid suction and wash, so as not to endanger the work being carried out.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-147.question: What do these lights mean?

options.a: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the red-and-white side; the red side is closed. Avoid suction and wash.
options.b: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the red-and-white side; the red side is closed. Passing at unreduced speed is possible.
options.c: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the red side; the red-and-white side is closed. Passing at unreduced speed is possible.
options.d: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the red side; the red-and-white side is closed. Avoid suction and wash.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-147.explanation: A vessel aground or sunk is marked with a combination of red and red-and-white lights that shows on which side it is safe to pass. The red-and-white side marks the permitted passage, while the plain red side remains closed; in addition, passing vessels must reduce speed to avoid suction and wash affecting the wrecked vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-148.question: What do these day signals mean?

options.a: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the red-and-white side; the red side is closed. Avoid suction and wash.
options.b: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the red-and-white side; the red side is closed. Passing at unreduced speed is possible.
options.c: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the red side; the red-and-white side is closed. Passing at unreduced speed is possible.
options.d: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the red side; the red-and-white side is closed. Avoid suction and wash.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-148.explanation: The daytime marking of a vessel aground or sunk follows the same principle: the red-and-white side indicates the permitted passage, the red side remains closed. Passing vessels must additionally reduce speed to avoid suction and wash, so as not to place further strain on the wrecked vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-149.question: What do these lights mean?

options.a: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the green side. Passing on the red side at unreduced speed is possible.
options.b: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the green side; the red side is closed. Avoid suction and wash.
options.c: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the red side; the green side is closed.
options.d: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the green side; the red side is closed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-149.explanation: Floating plant at work uses a green-and-red combination of lights to show on which side it is safe to pass: the green side marks the permitted passage, while the red side remains closed to traffic. This allows vessels to pass specifically on the safe side of the work site.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-150.question: What do these day signals mean?

options.a: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the green side. Passing on the red side at unreduced speed is possible.
options.b: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the red side; the green side is closed.
options.c: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the green side; the red side is closed. Avoid suction and wash.
options.d: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the green side; the red side is closed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-150.explanation: The day shapes for floating plant at work follow the same principle as the lights at night: green stands for the open side, red for the closed side. This lets the skipper recognise from a distance on which side it is safe to pass the work site.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-152.question: What do these lights mean?

options.a: Floating plant at work. Passing not permitted.
options.b: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on either side.
options.c: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing not permitted.
options.d: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the starboard side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-152.explanation: When floating plant at work shows a light combination without a one-sided closure, passing is permitted on either side. This differs from the marking of a vessel aground or sunk, where one side always remains closed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-153.question: What do these day signals mean?

options.a: Floating plant at work. Passing not permitted.
options.b: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on either side.
options.c: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing not permitted.
options.d: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the starboard side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-153.explanation: During the day as well, floating plant at work uses a corresponding combination of shapes to show whether passage is possible on both sides. If there is no closure marking for a particular side, vessels may pass on both port and starboard.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-154.question: What do these day signals mean?

options.a: Floating plant at work. Passing not permitted.
options.b: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing not permitted.
options.c: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on either side.
options.d: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the starboard side. Avoid suction and wash.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-154.explanation: This combination of signs again marks floating plant at work, where passing is permitted on either side. Other vessels must nevertheless stay alert and keep sufficient distance from the work site.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-162.question: What does this sound signal mean?

options.a: Turning (about) to starboard.
options.b: Course change to starboard.
options.c: Course change to port.
options.d: Turning (about) to port.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-162.explanation: Before turning around on the waterway, a vessel must announce this with a defined sound signal, since a turning manoeuvre takes up the entire width of the fairway and can otherwise be unexpectedly dangerous for other traffic. The signal shown announces that the vessel will turn to starboard, so that oncoming and following vessels can react in time.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-163.question: What does this sound signal mean?

options.a: Course change to starboard.
options.b: Course change to port.
options.c: Turning (about) to starboard.
options.d: Turning (about) to port.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-163.explanation: Just as with turning to starboard, a turning manoeuvre to port must also be announced in advance with a clear sound signal, so that other vessels in the fairway can make room or adjust their own course in time. The signal shown specifically stands for turning about to port and is distinct from the signals for a simple change of course.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-164.question: What does this sound signal mean?

options.a: Overtaking on the starboard side of the vessel ahead.
options.b: Harbour or side waterway; entering or leaving with a course change to starboard.
options.c: Harbour or side waterway; entering or leaving with a course change to port.
options.d: Overtaking on the port side of the vessel ahead.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-164.explanation: When overtaking on inland waterways, the overtaking vessel must announce in good time, by sound signal, on which side it intends to pass, so that the overtaken vessel can behave accordingly and the manoeuvre remains predictable for both. The signal shown announces that overtaking will take place on the starboard side of the vessel ahead.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-165.question: What does this sound signal mean?

options.a: Harbour or side waterway; entering or leaving with a course change to starboard.
options.b: Overtaking on the port side of the vessel ahead.
options.c: Overtaking on the starboard side of the vessel ahead.
options.d: Harbour or side waterway; entering or leaving with a course change to port.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-165.explanation: Just as with overtaking to starboard, there is a distinct sound signal for overtaking on the port side of the vessel ahead. This signal is necessary so that the overtaken vessel knows on which side to expect the overtaking vessel and does not steer into its path.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-166.question: What does this sound signal mean?

options.a: Harbour or side waterway; entering or leaving with a course change to port.
options.b: Overtaking on the port side of the vessel ahead.
options.c: Harbour or side waterway; entering or leaving with a course change to starboard.
options.d: Overtaking on the starboard side of the vessel ahead.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-166.explanation: A vessel wishing to enter or leave a harbour or side waterway while changing course to starboard must announce this to other traffic in good time by sound signal. Because such a manoeuvre crosses the main direction of travel, other vessels need this advance warning in order to react in time.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-167.question: What does this sound signal mean?

options.a: Overtaking on the port side of the vessel ahead.
options.b: Overtaking on the starboard side of the vessel ahead.
options.c: Harbour or side waterway; entering or leaving with a course change to port.
options.d: Harbour or side waterway; entering or leaving with a course change to starboard.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-167.explanation: As a mirror image of the signal for a course change to starboard, there is a distinct sound signal for entering or leaving a harbour or side waterway with a course change to port. Here too, the signal serves to warn crossing traffic in good time, since the manoeuvre takes the vessel off its normal course.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-170.question: What sound signals or signs must be given if the boat has become unable to manoeuvre?

options.a: Four short blasts. By day, wave a red flag; by night, wave a red light in the lower semicircle.
options.b: One long, four short blasts. By day, show a red flag; by night, show a red light.
options.c: Five short blasts. By day, wave a red flag; by night, wave a red light in the upper semicircle.
options.d: Give a group of short and long blasts at intervals. At night, switch on a red flashing light.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-170.explanation: If a boat has become unable to manoeuvre, for example due to engine or steering failure, this must be signalled immediately and unambiguously to other traffic, since the vessel poses an increased collision risk and can no longer give way itself. The prescribed signal is four short blasts, together with waving a red flag by day, or waving a red light in the lower semicircle by night, to make the vessel's position and distress situation visible.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-171.question: A vessel shows a blue board with a white flashing light on the starboard side of its wheelhouse. What does this signal mean?

options.a: Vessels are meeting on the starboard side. This signal need not be observed at all.
options.b: Vessels are meeting on the starboard side. This signal does not apply to small craft, but requires increased attention.
options.c: Vessels are meeting on the starboard side. This signal applies only to small craft.
options.d: Vessels are meeting on the starboard side. This signal also applies to all small craft.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-171.explanation: Large vessels that, for reasons related to the fairway, for example in tight bends, deviate from the usual port-to-port meeting rule and instead want to pass starboard-to-starboard show a blue board with a white flashing light on the starboard side to indicate this. This signal regulation is not binding on small craft, since their small size lets them easily keep clear; nevertheless, skippers of small craft must pay particular attention when they see this sign, because the large vessel is swinging across to the other side of the fairway.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-172.question: A sports boat follows a vessel that is not a small craft into the lock approach area. A vessel coming out of the lock chamber shows a blue board with a white flashing light on its starboard side. What does this sign mean?

options.a: The outgoing and incoming vessels pass each other on the port side; the small craft has priority.
options.b: The outgoing and incoming vessels pass each other on the starboard side; the small craft must wait.
options.c: The outgoing and incoming vessels pass each other on the starboard side; the small craft is only required to pay increased attention.
options.d: The outgoing and incoming vessels pass each other on the port side; the small craft is only required to pay increased attention.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-172.explanation: The rule of the blue sign with white flashing light also applies in the lock approach area: the vessel leaving the lock chamber and the vessel entering it pass each other on the starboard side instead of the usual port-to-port meeting. For the sports boat as a small craft, this sign does not create its own duty to wait, only a duty to pay increased attention, since it can easily keep clear of the larger vessel anyway.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-174.question: How must an overtaking manoeuvre be carried out?

options.a: Overtake swiftly. If necessary, accelerate the vessel strongly in order to pass quickly.
options.b: Overtake swiftly. Do not obstruct the vessels involved. Observe the traffic situation and any sound signals. Keep sufficient distance.
options.c: Overtake swiftly. Stay close along the bank; small craft must observe any sound signals.
options.d: Overtake swiftly; overtaking is only permitted on the starboard side, keep sufficient distance.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-174.explanation: An overtaking manoeuvre must be carried out swiftly, so the situation is not drawn out unnecessarily and both vessels return to normal running as soon as possible. In doing so, the vessels involved must not be obstructed, the general traffic situation and any sound signals must be observed, and sufficient safety distance must always be kept in order to avoid collisions or dangerous suction effects.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-182.question: A sailing vessel showing a black cone crosses, coming from the port side, the course of a power-driven vessel. Who must give way?

options.a: The sailing vessel with the black cone is not required to give way.
options.b: The sailing vessel with the black cone is required to give way.
options.c: The vessel without sails is required to give way.
options.d: Both vessels are required to give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-182.explanation: The black cone shows that the sailing vessel is also using its engine and is therefore legally classed as a power-driven vessel. In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, the one that has the other on her own starboard side must give way; since the motor-sailing vessel, approaching from the port side, sees the other power-driven vessel on her own starboard side, she is the one required to give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-183.question: Two small sailing craft, A and B, are on a collision course; A shows a black cone. Who must give way?

options.a: The vessel with the wind on the port side must give way.
options.b: Vessel A must give way.
options.c: Vessel B must give way.
options.d: The vessel that sees the other on its port side must give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-183.explanation: If one of two crossing small sailing craft shows a black cone, it counts as a power-driven vessel and no longer as a pure sailing vessel. The wind-side rule between sailing vessels does not apply here; instead the basic rule applies that power-driven vessels must give way to sailing vessels, so vessel A with the cone is the one required to give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-187.question: A small craft A is sailing downwind at night, running with the current, with the mainsail out to starboard. On the port beam, the green sidelight of a boat B is getting closer, showing no masthead light. Who must give way?

options.a: Boat B must give way, because vessel A is a small sailing craft with the wind on the port side.
options.b: Small craft A must give way. A boat with the wind on the port side must give way if it cannot clearly tell whether the vessel to windward has the wind on the starboard side.
options.c: Boat B must give way, because it is a small craft, and small craft must give way to other small sailing craft.
options.d: Small craft A must give way. A boat with the wind on the starboard side must give way if it cannot clearly tell whether the vessel to windward has the wind on the port side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-187.explanation: When two sailing vessels are on a collision course and one cannot reliably tell which side the other has the wind on, a precautionary rule applies: a vessel with the wind on the port side must give way as long as it cannot clearly establish that the vessel to windward also has the wind on the port side. Since boat B shows no masthead light, it is presumably also a sailing vessel, but its wind side is not clearly identifiable to A, so A must give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-192.question: A small sailing craft crosses the fairway at night. On the port side, the following lights of a vessel appear, which wants to cross the course of the small sailing craft at an acute angle. What do these lights mean?

options.a: Freely navigating ferry.
options.b: Pushed convoy, seen from ahead.
options.c: Small craft with mechanical propulsion.
options.d: Towed small craft.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-192.explanation: The combination described, a single masthead light together with red and green sidelights and no additional special-purpose signals, corresponds exactly to the prescribed lighting of a small power-driven vessel at night. These standard lights clearly distinguish it from a ferry, a pushed convoy, or a towed vessel, each of which must show its own, different combination of lights.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-193.question: A small sailing craft crosses the fairway at night. Off the port side, the following lights appear on a vessel that intends to cross the sailing craft's course at an acute angle. Who must give way?

options.a: The small craft under sail.
options.b: Both must give way.
options.c: The power-driven small craft.
options.d: The small craft that has the other vessel on its port side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-193.explanation: Among recreational craft, sailing vessels generally have right of way over power-driven small craft because they are more limited in their ability to manoeuvre. Since the motor craft is crossing the fairway at an acute angle and approaching the sailing boat from the port side, under the give-way rules it is the power-driven small craft that must keep clear. It must alter course and/or speed early and clearly to avoid a collision.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-195.question: A small sailing craft is crossing the fairway at night. A vessel is approaching from astern showing a bicolour lantern and a masthead light. What do these lights mean?

options.a: Small craft without mechanical propulsion.
options.b: Small craft under sail.
options.c: Power-driven small craft.
options.d: Small craft under sail with engine also running.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-195.explanation: A vessel that shows a combined bicolour lantern (red to port, green to starboard) together with a white masthead light at night is identifying itself as a power-driven small craft. A vessel under sail alone shows only its sidelights (often combined in one bicolour lantern) and a sternlight, but never a masthead light, since that light is reserved for craft under mechanical propulsion. The vessel approaching from astern with this light combination must therefore be a motorboat.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-196.question: What do the following lights mean at night on an inland waterway?

options.a: Passage permitted for small craft.
options.b: Waterway closed to shipping.
options.c: Avoid wash and suction.
options.d: No passage for small craft.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-196.explanation: Certain vessels and floating installations that are especially vulnerable to wash and suction (such as ferries, work craft, or protected areas) mark themselves at night with a special light signal telling passing traffic to take care. The light pattern shown is the night-time equivalent of the daytime board sign "avoid wash and suction," and it requires passing vessels to reduce speed so that no dangerous waves or suction effects are created.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-210.question: What sound signal must be given when help is needed in an emergency?

options.a: Repeated short blasts, no bell strokes.
options.b: Repeated long blasts, or groups of bell strokes.
options.c: Three short blasts, no bell strokes.
options.d: One long blast, occasional bell strokes.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-210.explanation: The international distress signal on inland waterways includes repeated long blasts or groups of bell strokes, because these are clearly different from the short signals used for course and manoeuvring communication. This ensures that a call for help cannot be confused with other sound signals, such as overtaking signals. Other vessels within hearing range must respond to such a signal and render assistance where possible.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-211.question: What does circular waving of a red flag by day mean on a vessel?

options.a: A vessel in distress trying to call for help by visual signal.
options.b: A vessel restricted in its ability to manoeuvre trying to call for help by visual signal.
options.c: No meaning for passing shipping traffic.
options.d: A vessel requiring protection, avoid wash and suction.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-211.explanation: Waving a red flag in a circular motion during daylight (or, failing that, any other object) is one of the internationally recognised distress signals and indicates that a vessel is in distress and urgently needs help. Other water users must take such a signal seriously, approach the vessel in difficulty, and render assistance if it is safe to do so, or alert the rescue coordination centre.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-212.question: What distress signals can a windsurfer give on inland waterways?

options.a: Circular waving of the arms is to be avoided; the sail should be held as vertical as possible.
options.b: Repeated long groups of bell strokes.
options.c: Circular waving of a green flag that cannot be confused with other signals.
options.d: Circular waving of the arms or of an object.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-212.explanation: Because a windsurfer cannot carry flags, lights, or sound equipment, the prescribed distress signal is simply waving the arms, or an object held in the hand, in a circular motion. This simple, widely visible signal follows the same logic as the general distress signal of circular waving and can easily be recognised by other vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-246.question: What lights does a pushed convoy carry?

options.a: Three white masthead lights in a horizontal row, the sidelights, and three white sternlights in a horizontal row.
options.b: Three white masthead lights arranged in a triangle, the sidelights, and two white sternlights in a horizontal row.
options.c: Three white masthead lights arranged vertically one above another, the sidelights, and three white sternlights in a horizontal row.
options.d: Three white masthead lights arranged in a triangle, the sidelights, and three white sternlights in a horizontal row.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-246.explanation: To indicate its size and shape, a pushed convoy shows at night three white masthead lights arranged in a triangle, in addition to the sidelights and three white sternlights placed side by side in a horizontal row. This distinctive light pattern distinguishes a pushed convoy from a single vessel or a towed convoy and lets other traffic recognise the type, size, and heading of the convoy from its lights alone.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-249.question: What does marking a vessel with a red-and-white flag mean, and what must be observed?

options.a: Vessel requiring protection, maintain wash and avoid suction.
options.b: Vessel requiring protection, maintain speed and avoid wash and suction.
options.c: Vessel requiring protection, reduce speed and avoid wash and suction.
options.d: Vessel requiring protection, reduce speed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-249.explanation: A red-and-white flag marks a vessel that requires special protection, for example one engaged in diving, surveying, or sounding operations. Other vessels must reduce speed and keep sufficient distance in such cases to avoid wash and suction, so as not to endanger the work being carried out or any persons in the water.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-250.question: What visual signal may be given by day instead of four short blasts?

options.a: Wave a red flag through the lower half-circle.
options.b: Show a red flag.
options.c: Wave a red flag through the upper half-circle.
options.d: Wave a red flag in a full circle.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-250.explanation: Four short blasts is the sound signal used by a vessel that is not under command or is restricted in its ability to manoeuvre, to draw attention to itself or request priority. When this sound signal cannot be given during daylight, or needs to be reinforced, the equivalent visual signal is waving a red flag through the lower half-circle, conveying the same meaning.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-265.question: What action should be taken if the rudder breaks on a dinghy?

options.a: Anchor immediately and send a distress call, hoist a signal shape (blue cone).
options.b: Wave a red flag in a circular motion, keep a tow line ready.
options.c: Use an emergency rudder or paddle as a substitute, leave the fairway, make yourself recognisable as not under command.
options.d: Take down the sail, start the engine, and steer for the bank in reverse.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-265.explanation: If the rudder breaks on a dinghy, manoeuvrability must be restored as quickly as possible, for example using an emergency rudder or a paddle. At the same time the boat should leave the fairway so as not to endanger other traffic, and should make itself recognisable - for instance by signal or call - as temporarily not under command, so that other vessels can keep clear accordingly.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-175.question: When does a risk of collision exist?

options.a: When two vessels approach each other and neither vessel's course changes.
options.b: When two vessels approach each other on a constant bearing.
options.c: When two vessels approach each other and both alter course to starboard.
options.d: When two vessels approach each other and one vessel's course changes.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-175.explanation: A risk of collision exists in particular when two vessels are approaching each other and the bearing of the other vessel remains nearly constant over time (a steady bearing). If, on the other hand, the bearing changes noticeably, the vessels will generally pass clear of each other. This fundamental rule of collision avoidance applies regardless of whether one's own or the other vessel's course changes, and it forms the basis for taking early and unambiguous avoiding action.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-59.question: Under what conditions may a sportboat with an electric motor be operated without a licence?

options.a: The drive power is at most 7.5 kilowatts in continuous duty mode (S1).
options.b: It may always be operated without a licence, regardless of drive power.
options.c: Up to a drive power of 11.03 kilowatts in continuous duty mode (S1).
options.d: It may never be operated without a licence, regardless of drive power.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-59.explanation: Sportboats with electric propulsion may be operated without a licence as long as the drive power does not exceed a limit of 7.5 kilowatts in continuous duty mode (S1). This threshold is the electric-motor equivalent of the 11.03 kW (15 hp) limit for combustion engines, since an electric motor in continuous operation produces comparable thrust at a lower rated power.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-73.question: For which sportboats is the inland-waterway sportboat licence required?

options.a: For sportboats with more than 11.03 kW (15 hp) net power using a combustion engine, or 7.5 kW using an electric motor in continuous duty (S1), and more than 20 m in length.
options.b: For sportboats with less than 11.03 kW (15 hp) net power using a combustion engine, or 7.5 kW using an electric motor in continuous duty (S1), and more than 20 m in length.
options.c: For sportboats with less than 11.03 kW (15 hp) net power using a combustion engine, or 7.5 kW using an electric motor in continuous duty (S1), and less than 20 m in length.
options.d: For sportboats with more than 11.03 kW (15 hp) net power using a combustion engine, or 7.5 kW using an electric motor in continuous duty (S1), and less than 20 m in length.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-73.explanation: The inland sportboat licence is compulsory for sportboats whose engine develops more than 11.03 kW (15 hp) for combustion engines, or more than 7.5 kW for electric motors in continuous duty (S1), provided the boat is also less than 20 m long. From a length of 20 m upward a higher-level qualification (Sportschifferzeugnis or Sportpatent) is required instead, while below the stated power thresholds no licence is needed at all.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-74.question: On which waters does the inland-waterway sportboat licence apply?

options.a: On all sea waterways.
options.b: On all state (Länder) waters.
options.c: On the federal waterways and all state waters.
options.d: On the federal waterways in the inland area.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-74.explanation: The scope of the inland sportboat licence covers federal inland waterways, i.e. the rivers, canals, and lakes in the interior of the country administered by the federal government. State-level waters (such as many smaller lakes) fall under state law instead and may have their own, sometimes differing requirements, which is why the federal licence does not automatically apply there.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-75.question: For which reasons must the inland-waterway sportboat licence be withdrawn?

options.a: For lack of reliability following a committed regulatory offence.
options.b: For doubtful reliability due to age.
options.c: For lack of fitness or lack of reliability.
options.d: For doubtful fitness due to alcohol abuse.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-75.explanation: The inland sportboat licence must be withdrawn whenever the holder no longer possesses the physical or mental fitness, or the personal reliability, required to operate a sportboat. Both are basic prerequisites for holding the licence, so their permanent loss necessarily leads to withdrawal of the licence, regardless of individual minor offences or age alone.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-78.question: Besides physical and mental fitness and professional competence, what requirements must the operator of a sportboat on inland waterways meet, if the maximum net power of the engine is 11.03 kW or less for combustion engines, or 7.5 kW or less for electric motors in continuous duty (S1)?

options.a: Minimum age 16.
options.b: Holding an inland-waterway sportboat licence for power-driven sportboats, or an equivalent certificate of competence.
options.c: Minimum age 14.
options.d: Proof of reliability.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-78.explanation: Anyone operating a sportboat with drive power up to 11.03 kW (combustion engine) or up to 7.5 kW (electric motor, S1) on inland waterways does not need a sportboat licence, but must nevertheless have reached a minimum age of 16. Physical, mental, and professional suitability are therefore not verified through an exam here, but are simply assumed to be covered by the age requirement.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-79.question: Besides physical and mental fitness and professional competence, what requirements must the operator of a sportboat on the Rhine meet, if the engine's net power exceeds 11.03 kW for combustion engines, or 7.5 kW for electric motors in continuous duty (S1)?

options.a: Minimum age 16.
options.b: Holding an inland-waterway sportboat licence for power-driven sportboats, or an equivalent certificate of competence.
options.c: At least 14 years old.
options.d: Proof of reliability.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-79.explanation: A stricter rule applies on the Rhine than on other inland waterways: anyone operating a sportboat there with drive power exceeding 11.03 kW (or more than 7.5 kW for electric motors) must hold the inland sportboat licence for power-driven boats or an equivalent certificate of competence. Unlike below the power threshold, a minimum age alone is not sufficient here.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-80.question: What requirements apply to the person with whom the skipper wants to share the helm of a power-driven sportboat on inland waterways?

options.a: That person must be at least 16 years old and physically, mentally, and professionally fit.
options.b: That person must be at least 16 years old and hold the inland-waterway sportboat licence for power-driven sportboats.
options.c: That person must be at least 14 years old and physically, mentally, and professionally fit.
options.d: That person must be at least 18 years old and physically, mentally, and professionally fit.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-80.explanation: If the skipper of a power-driven sportboat temporarily hands the helm to another person, that person must be at least 16 years old and physically, mentally, and professionally fit, but does not need to hold a sportboat licence of their own as long as the responsible skipper remains on board and in charge. Overall responsibility for operating the vessel stays with the licence holder.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-83.question: Up to what vessel length does the inland-waterway sportboat licence authorise operating a sportboat on inland waterways?

options.a: Up to a length of less than 15 m (including rudder and bowsprit).
options.b: Up to a length of less than 25 m (including rudder and bowsprit).
options.c: Up to a length of less than 20 m (excluding rudder and bowsprit).
options.d: Up to a length of less than 25 m (excluding rudder and bowsprit).

sportboot-binnen-elwis-83.explanation: The inland sportboat licence entitles the holder to operate sportboats up to a length of less than 20 m, whereby fixed parts projecting beyond the hull, such as the rudder and bowsprit, are not counted in this length measurement. From a hull length of 20 m upward, a higher-level qualification (Sportschifferzeugnis or Sportpatent) is required.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-226.question: On which waters is a licence required to operate a sportboat under sail?

options.a: On all state (Länder) waters.
options.b: On all German waterways.
options.c: On certain waterways in Berlin and Brandenburg.
options.d: On inland waterways and all state waters.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-226.explanation: In principle, no licence is required to operate a sportboat under sail on inland waterways. An exception, however, applies to certain waterways in Berlin and Brandenburg specified under state law, where a licence requirement also applies to sailing boats for reasons of traffic density and safety.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-228.question: Which certificate of competence authorises operating a sportboat up to 25 m in length on the Rhine?

options.a: The inland-waterway sportboat licence.
options.b: The Sportpatent.
options.c: The Sportschifferzeugnis.
options.d: The sea-waterway sportboat licence.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-228.explanation: On the Rhine, it is specifically the Sportpatent that authorises operation of sportboats up to 25 m in length, since the dense commercial traffic and particular current conditions there demand higher professional qualifications than the standard inland sportboat licence. The basic SBF Binnen does not cover larger and faster sportboats on the Rhine.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-229.question: Which certificate of competence authorises operating a sportboat between 20 m and 25 m in length on inland waterways outside the Rhine?

options.a: The inland-waterway sportboat licence.
options.b: The sea-waterway sportboat licence.
options.c: The Sportschifferzeugnis or the Sportpatent.
options.d: The inland-waterway sportboat licence for power-driven sportboats or the Sportpatent.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-229.explanation: For sportboats between 20 and 25 m in length on inland waterways outside the Rhine, the basic inland sportboat licence is no longer sufficient; instead, either the Sportschifferzeugnis or the Sportpatent is required, since these higher-level qualifications demonstrate the more extensive knowledge needed for larger vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-232.question: What types of identification marks exist for sportboats?

options.a: Official registration marks and officially recognised registration marks.
options.b: Only officially recognised registration marks.
options.c: Marking according to the declaration of conformity (CE mark).
options.d: Only official registration marks.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-232.explanation: Sportboats can be identified in two different ways: through official registration marks (issued by state registers such as the inland or sea shipping register) or through officially recognised marks issued by private, state-approved associations or clubs (for example via the International Certificate for Pleasure Craft). Both forms of identification are legally equivalent.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-234.question: What do officially recognised registration marks consist of?

options.a: The European vessel identification number, followed by the code letter of the issuing organisation.
options.b: The number from the sea vessel register, followed by the code letter of the issuing organisation.
options.c: The number of the International Certificate for Pleasure Craft, followed by the code letter of the issuing organisation.
options.d: The number from the inland vessel register, followed by the code letter of the issuing organisation.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-234.explanation: Officially recognised registration marks consist of the number of the International Certificate for Pleasure Craft, followed by a code letter identifying the issuing organisation. This combination allows authorities to clearly trace a sportboat back to its issuing body and owner without the need for an official state register.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-17.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: No meeting/passing for vessels over 20 m in length.
options.b: No meeting/passing.
options.c: No overtaking.
options.d: No overtaking for vessels under 20 m in length.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-17.explanation: The board sign shown belongs to the group of prohibition signs and generally forbids any overtaking in the marked stretch. Such prohibitions are mainly put up at confusing, narrow, or heavily used sections of the waterway, where an overtaking manoeuvre could lead to dangerous encounter situations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-18.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: No overtaking; oncoming traffic must be expected.
options.b: No meeting/passing for vessels over 12 m in length.
options.c: No meeting/passing at a narrow passage.
options.d: No overtaking for all vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-18.explanation: This prohibition sign marks a narrow section where two vessels cannot safely pass each other. Within the affected stretch, no vessel may therefore meet an oncoming one; vessels must wait until the narrow passage is clear before entering it.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-19.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: Hazardous shoreline area, risk of being swept over; minimum passing distance 100 m.
options.b: Waterway that can be navigated safely at all times; no danger from waves.
options.c: Avoid wash and suction.
options.d: Waterway that cannot be navigated safely at all times; danger from waves.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-19.explanation: This sign indicates that particular care must be taken to avoid wash and suction in the area concerned, for example because the banks, installations, or other vessels there are especially sensitive to it. Vessels must adjust their speed accordingly to avoid causing damaging waves or suction effects.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-20.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: Maximum distance in metres to be maintained on the following stretch from the location of the sign.
options.b: Maximum speed in km/h not to be exceeded on the fairway side to the right in the direction of travel.
options.c: Minimum distance in metres to be maintained on the following stretch from the location of the sign.
options.d: Narrowing of the fairway to 40 m.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-20.explanation: This sign specifies a minimum distance in metres that must be maintained on the stretch following the point where the board is placed, for example distance from the bank or from a structure. It serves to protect banks, structures, or other sensitive areas from vessels passing too close.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-21.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: Permanent closure of a section of the waterway.
options.b: Requirement to stop before movable bridges, barrages, and locks.
options.c: No further passage for sport craft.
options.d: Requirement to sound one long signal.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-21.explanation: This sign is a mandatory sign that requires vessels to stop before movable bridges, barrages, or locks until passage is authorised. It serves safety purposes, since these structures may be temporarily closed or in motion, and an uncontrolled approach could lead to serious accidents.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-22.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: Anchoring prohibited for all vessels.
options.b: Anchoring and mooring prohibited.
options.c: Anchoring prohibited for small craft of 12 m and above.
options.d: Anchoring prohibited for small craft under 12 m.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-22.explanation: This prohibition sign forbids all vessels - regardless of size or type of propulsion - from anchoring in the marked area. Such prohibitions often apply near underwater pipelines or cables, or in narrow parts of the fairway, where an anchored vessel would obstruct or endanger through traffic.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-23.question: What do the following board signs mean?

options.a: Mooring and lying prohibited for commercial vessels.
options.b: Mooring and lying prohibited for sportboats.
options.c: Mooring and lying prohibited for sportboats over 12 m in length.
options.d: Mooring and lying prohibited.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-23.explanation: This sign generally prohibits all vessels from mooring and lying in the marked area, without distinguishing by vessel type or size. Such prohibitions are used, for example, to keep banks, entrances, or areas with particular traffic from being obstructed by moored vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-24.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: Sound one short and one long blast.
options.b: Sound two long blasts.
options.c: Sound one long blast.
options.d: Sound one short blast.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-24.explanation: This mandatory sign requires vessels to sound one long blast before reaching the marked point, usually to make themselves known to oncoming traffic at a blind bend or narrow passage. The long blast thus serves to prevent collisions at locations with restricted visibility.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-25.question: What do the following board signs mean?

options.a: Practice course requiring a permit for waterskiing or personal watercraft.
options.b: Water areas where waterskiing or personal watercraft may be operated.
options.c: Practice course not requiring a permit for waterskiing or personal watercraft.
options.d: Waterskiing and personal watercraft permitted. Water-skiers and personal watercraft have right of way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-25.explanation: This sign marks water areas where waterskiing or riding personal watercraft is expressly permitted, while such activity is generally prohibited outside these marked areas. This concentrates these activities, which can pose a hazard to other water users, in suitably designated zones.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-26.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: Crossing the fairway is permitted.
options.b: End of a mandatory or prohibited stretch.
options.c: Changing sides of the fairway is permitted.
options.d: Section of a ferry route that is not free-running.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-26.explanation: This sign marks the end of a stretch previously designated by a mandatory or prohibition sign. From this point on, the earlier restriction or requirement no longer applies, unless a new sign imposes a different rule.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-27.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: Prohibition of passage and closure for small craft.
options.b: Prohibition of passage and closure of the stretch to shipping.
options.c: Prohibition of passage, but navigable by small craft without an engine.
options.d: Prohibition of passage, but navigable by small craft with the engine switched off.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-27.explanation: This sign completely closes the marked stretch to shipping; passage is prohibited for all vessels without exception. Such closures are ordered, for example, because of construction work, accidents, or other exceptional hazardous situations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-28.question: What do the following shipping signals mean?

options.a: Bridge, barrage, or lock closed.
options.b: Installation permanently closed.
options.c: Stop signal for all vessels.
options.d: Exceptional obstruction to shipping.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-28.explanation: The signal shown at a bridge, barrage, or lock means that the structure is currently closed and passage is not possible. Vessels must wait in front of the structure until a different signal indicates that it has opened and passage is permitted.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-29.question: What do the following shipping signals mean?

options.a: Bridge, barrage, or lock closed.
options.b: Exceptional obstruction to shipping.
options.c: Stop signal for all vessels.
options.d: Installation permanently closed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-29.explanation: In contrast to a merely temporary closure, this signal indicates that the bridge, barrage, or lock in question is permanently closed to shipping, for example due to being taken out of service or a defect. In this case vessels must choose an alternative route.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-36.question: How should one behave when meeting other vessels in a narrow fairway?

options.a: The vessel travelling with the current must stop.
options.b: The vessel travelling against the current must give way.
options.c: Reduce speed and maintain a sufficient passing distance.
options.d: Increase speed to complete the passing manoeuvre quickly.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-36.explanation: In a narrow fairway there is often not enough room to pass safely at unchanged speed. The general rule therefore requires reducing speed in good time and maintaining a sufficient passing distance, in order to avoid suction, wash, and the risk of collision.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-88.question: What is understood by 'fairway'?

options.a: It is the part of the waterway bounded by the banks.
options.b: The part of the waterway that, according to local conditions, is used by through shipping traffic.
options.c: It is the part of the waterway where the depth is 2.50 m or more.
options.d: The part of the waterway in which specific widths and depths are maintained or aimed for, for through shipping traffic.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-88.explanation: Legally, the "fairway" is the part of the waterway that is actually used by through traffic according to local conditions - independent of exact depth or bank measurements. This definition matters because many right-of-way and give-way rules are specifically tied to use of the fairway, such as the priority of an upstream-bound vessel within the fairway over vessels outside it.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-100.question: What does a red-and-green striped buoy or spar mean, and what must be observed?

options.a: Bifurcation of the channel. Passing only permitted on the starboard side.
options.b: Bifurcation of the channel. Passing permitted on both sides.
options.c: Bifurcation of the channel. Keep to the right in the direction of travel.
options.d: Bifurcation of the channel. Keep to the left in the direction of travel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-100.explanation: A red-and-green striped buoy or spar marks a bifurcation of the channel, i.e. a point where the fairway splits into two equally valid branches. Unlike one-sided lateral marks, this buoy may be passed on either side, since both branches of the fairway are navigable.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-107.question: What does this board sign mean?

options.a: Berth for vessels carrying flammable substances, prohibited for small craft.
options.b: Berth for all vessels, prohibited for small craft.
options.c: Berth for vessels carrying explosive substances, prohibited for small craft.
options.d: Berth for vessels carrying substances hazardous to health, prohibited for small craft.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-107.explanation: This board sign marks a berth reserved exclusively for vessels carrying explosive substances on board. For safety reasons, this berth is generally off-limits to small craft, so as not to expose them to the particular hazard posed by the dangerous-goods vessels moored there.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-108.question: What do these board signs mean?

options.a: Berth for vessels without dangerous goods, also for small craft.
options.b: Berth for vessels without dangerous goods, not for small craft.
options.c: Berth for vessels with dangerous goods, not for small craft.
options.d: Berth for vessels with dangerous goods, also for small craft.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-108.explanation: This board sign marks a berth for vessels without dangerous goods on board, which small craft are expressly permitted to use as well. Since no dangerous-goods vessels lie there, there is no reason to exclude sportboats from this berth.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-110.question: What does the following board sign mean?

options.a: Recommended passage span, passage permitted in both directions.
options.b: Passage is permitted only through this bridge span and only in one direction.
options.c: Recommended passage, passage in the opposite direction prohibited.
options.d: Passage is permitted only through this bridge span and in both directions.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-110.explanation: This sign at a bridge marks a recommended, but not mandatory, passage span that may be used in both directions. Other spans of the bridge are not thereby forbidden, but the marked span generally offers the most favourable conditions for passage.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-111.question: What do the following board signs mean?

options.a: Passage is permitted only through this bridge span and only in one direction.
options.b: Passage is permitted only through this bridge span and in both directions.
options.c: Recommended passage span, passage permitted in both directions.
options.d: Recommended passage, passage in the opposite direction prohibited.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-111.explanation: This sign likewise marks a recommended passage span, but with the additional restriction that passage in the opposite direction is not permitted. Vessels may therefore only use the span in the direction indicated by the sign.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-112.question: What do these board signs at bridges mean?

options.a: Recommended passage only between the two boards.
options.b: Passage permitted only between the two boards.
options.c: Recommended passage with oncoming traffic.
options.d: Passage permitted only outside the two boards.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-112.explanation: When two such board signs are mounted at a bridge, passage is mandatorily permitted only in the area between these two boards. This is a binding requirement, not merely a recommendation, so vessels may not pass through the bridge outside this marked area.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-113.question: What do these board signs at bridges mean?

options.a: Recommended passage with oncoming traffic.
options.b: Passage permitted only between the two boards.
options.c: Recommended passage only between the two boards.
options.d: Passage permitted only outside the two boards.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-113.explanation: Similar to question 112, a passage area between two boards is marked here, but this is only a recommended route rather than a binding requirement. Passing outside the boards is therefore not strictly prohibited, but is less advisable.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-114.question: What does this board sign at bridges mean?

options.a: Recommended passage in one direction only.
options.b: Recommended passage with oncoming traffic.
options.c: Passage permitted only alongside the board.
options.d: Recommended passage without oncoming traffic.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-114.explanation: This board sign at a bridge indicates a recommended passage span in which oncoming traffic must be expected. Vessel operators must adjust their navigation accordingly and be prepared for encounters within the span.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-115.question: What do these board signs at bridges mean?

options.a: Recommended passage with oncoming traffic.
options.b: Recommended passage in both directions.
options.c: Passage permitted only outside the two boards.
options.d: Recommended passage without oncoming traffic.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-115.explanation: In contrast to question 114, this sign indicates a recommended passage span in which no oncoming traffic is to be expected. Vessels can therefore use this span without needing to anticipate vessels coming the other way through the same opening.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-116.question: What does this board sign mean in the area of a weir?

options.a: Closed water area, but navigable by small craft with an engine.
options.b: Prohibition of passage and closure of the stretch to shipping.
options.c: Installation requiring protection.
options.d: Closed water area, but navigable by small craft without an engine.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-116.explanation: In the area of a weir, this sign indicates a prohibition of passage and a complete closure of the stretch to shipping, since a weir can be life-threatening for vessels (strong current, turbulence, a drop in water level). Passage is therefore fundamentally forbidden to all vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-151.question: What do the following signs in the fairway mean?

options.a: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the side with the red-white-red board sign; the green-white-green side is closed.
options.b: Vessel aground or sunk. Passing permitted on the side with the green-white-green board sign; the red-white-red side is closed. Avoid wash and suction.
options.c: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the side with the green-white-green board sign; the red-white-red side is closed.
options.d: Floating plant at work. Passing permitted on the side with the green-white-green board sign; the red-white-red side is closed. Avoid wash and suction.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-151.explanation: A floating work craft (such as a dredger or crane) is marked on both sides with board signs: the side showing the green-white-green sign may be passed, while the side showing the red-white-red sign is closed. This ensures that passing vessels do not endanger the work craft or the people working on it.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-156.question: What does this board sign mean?

options.a: Closed water area, prohibition of passage and closure of the stretch to shipping.
options.b: Closed water area, not navigable by small craft.
options.c: Closed water area, but navigable by small craft with the engine switched off.
options.d: Closed water area, but navigable by small craft without an engine.
