sportboot-binnen-elwis-156.explanation: This sign generally closes the marked water area, but allows an exception for small craft without mechanical propulsion, such as rowing or paddle boats and sailing boats with the engine off. These may use the area because they pose less of a hazard than vessels under mechanical power.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-157.question: What does this board sign mean?

options.a: No-navigation zone for small craft with mechanical propulsion.
options.b: No-navigation zone for vessels with mechanical propulsion.
options.c: No-navigation zone for small craft without a running engine.
options.d: No-navigation zone for vessels without an engine.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-157.explanation: This sign prohibits all vessels with mechanical propulsion - not just small craft, but in principle any motorised vessel - from using the marked area. Vessels without mechanical propulsion, such as sailing, rowing, or paddle boats, are not affected by this prohibition.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-158.question: How is a protected swimming zone marked?

options.a: By red buoys.
options.b: By green buoys.
options.c: By yellow buoys.
options.d: By buoys striped red and green.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-158.explanation: Protected swimming zones on inland waterways are marked with yellow buoys, since yellow is the special colour used for restricted and protected areas that lie outside the normal fairway buoyage. This marking warns vessels to avoid the area or to proceed with particular caution so as not to endanger swimmers.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-190.question: What is the priority if a dinghy has capsized and cannot be righted again?

options.a: Immediately give the prescribed distress signals and try by all means to get the vessel out of the fairway.
options.b: Put on lifejackets and summon help by suitable means. If necessary, take down the sails.
options.c: Climb onto the capsized boat and stay calm to minimise heat loss. If that is not possible, swim to the nearest shore and get help.
options.d: Check that the whole crew is present, assist if necessary. Hold on to the boat or, if possible, lie on it, and wait for help.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-190.explanation: Basic seamanship rules state that after an unrecoverable capsize, crew should stay with the boat, since it provides buoyancy and is much easier for rescuers to spot than people in the water. The first step is a headcount of the crew and mutual assistance if needed, after which everyone should hold on to or lie on the hull and wait for help.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-197.question: Where must speed be reduced to avoid suction and wash?

options.a: Before harbour entrances, at loading, unloading and mooring places, near cable ferries, on marked stretches, near floating equipment at work.
options.b: Before harbour entrances, at loading, unloading and mooring places, near cable ferries, on marked stretches, near floating navigation marks.
options.c: Before entrances (in general), at loading, unloading and mooring places, near cable ferries, on marked stretches, near floating equipment at work.
options.d: Before harbour entrances, at loading, unloading and mooring places, near free-running ferries, on marked stretches, near floating equipment at work.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-197.explanation: Under the BinSchStrO, speed must be set so as to avoid suction and wash, especially before harbour entrances, at loading/unloading points and moorings, near ferries that are not free-running (e.g. cable ferries), on specially marked stretches, and near floating equipment such as dredgers that are working. These locations are particularly vulnerable to wash, since people, structures or equipment there could be endangered.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-198.question: What does this panel sign mean?

options.a: Recommended direction of travel.
options.b: Prescribed direction of travel, only for small craft.
options.c: Prescribed direction of travel.
options.d: Travel to the left prohibited.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-198.explanation: The round blue mandatory sign with a white arrow indicates the prescribed direction of travel that every vessel must follow; it is not merely a recommendation. It is used to safely direct traffic on confusing or narrow stretches of waterway.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-199.question: What does the sign below mean when the red light is showing?

options.a: Prohibition of entry into a harbour or secondary waterway.
options.b: Prohibition of overtaking on this stretch.
options.c: Caution, twin lock, left chamber closed.
options.d: Caution, exit from harbour or secondary fairway.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-199.explanation: At harbour mouths or secondary waterways, traffic is often controlled by light signals; a red light on this sign means that entering the harbour or secondary waterway is prohibited. This prevents collisions with traffic on the main waterway or with vessels leaving the harbour.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-200.question: What does this panel sign mean?

options.a: 10 km/h for larger vessels.
options.b: 10 km/h maximum speed for small craft.
options.c: 10 km/h maximum speed relative to the current.
options.d: 10 km/h maximum speed relative to the bank.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-200.explanation: Unless stated otherwise, speed limits shown on panel signs refer to speed over ground, i.e. relative to the bank, not to speed through the water. This matters because wash and suction depend on actual progress over ground, so this protects the banks, structures, and other water users.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-201.question: What does this panel sign mean?

options.a: Requirement: sound a warning signal.
options.b: Requirement: proceed straight ahead.
options.c: Requirement: exercise particular caution.
options.d: Requirement: stop before the sign.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-201.explanation: The mandatory sign with an exclamation mark requires particular caution on the stretch in question, without prescribing a specific action such as stopping or sounding a signal. It is typically posted before blind bends, narrow points, or junctions.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-202.question: What does this panel sign mean?

options.a: Turning prohibited in the middle of the fairway.
options.b: Turning prohibited.
options.c: Prohibited direction of travel, right or left.
options.d: Prohibited to travel in both indicated directions.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-202.explanation: This panel sign indicates a general prohibition on turning, posted at locations where a turning manoeuvre would significantly endanger other traffic, for example in narrow or heavily used stretches of the fairway.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-203.question: What does this panel sign mean?

options.a: Recommended turning place. Small craft may lie stopped there.
options.b: Recommended turning place. Stopping is prohibited for all vessels.
options.c: Prescribed turning place. Stopping is prohibited for all vessels.
options.d: Prescribed turning place. Small craft may lie stopped there.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-203.explanation: This sign marks a recommended (not mandatory) turning place where, however, stopping is strictly prohibited for all vessels, so that the area remains clear for turning manoeuvres.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-204.question: What does this panel sign mean?

options.a: Lift bridge.
options.b: Weir.
options.c: Lock.
options.d: Safety gate.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-204.explanation: This panel sign marks a weir, a barrage structure used to regulate water levels, which is generally not navigable and whose surroundings pose an increased hazard due to current and suction.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-221.question: Where is waterskiing permitted on inland waterways?

options.a: Outside the fairway.
options.b: Anywhere, as long as shipping is not endangered.
options.c: Outside the navigable channel.
options.d: Only in areas released for it by a panel sign.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-221.explanation: Waterskiing on inland waterways is only permitted in areas explicitly released by a corresponding panel sign, since the activity poses a particular hazard to other traffic due to high speeds and the tow line involved.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-224.question: Under what conditions may a personal watercraft be operated outside designated stretches/water areas?

options.a: As long as no other water user is obstructed.
options.b: At large special events, outside the navigable channel.
options.c: Above high-water mark I, only within the fairway.
options.d: During touring/cruising runs with a clear, straight course.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-224.explanation: Outside designated stretches or water areas, personal watercraft may only be operated as part of touring or cruising runs on a clear, straight course, since this avoids the sudden turns, crossing manoeuvres or jumps that could endanger other water users.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-239.question: A vessel is travelling downstream. Ahead lies a red buoy. On which side of the fairway is this buoy, and on which side of the vessel must it be passed?

options.a: It is on the right side of the fairway and must be passed on the port side of the vessel.
options.b: It is on the left side of the fairway and must be passed on the starboard side of the vessel.
options.c: It is on the right side of the fairway and must be passed on the starboard side of the vessel.
options.d: It is on the left side of the fairway and must be passed on the port side of the vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-239.explanation: In the European inland buoyage system, red buoys are laid out with reference to the downstream direction: they mark the right-hand side of the fairway as seen when travelling downstream. A vessel travelling downstream must therefore pass the red buoy on its starboard side, leaving the buoy to port.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-240.question: A vessel is travelling upstream. Ahead lies a red buoy. On which side of the fairway is this buoy, and on which side of the vessel must it be passed?

options.a: It is on the left side of the fairway and must be passed on the port side of the vessel.
options.b: It is on the right side of the fairway and must be passed on the port side of the vessel.
options.c: It is on the right side of the fairway and must be passed on the starboard side of the vessel.
options.d: It is on the left side of the fairway and must be passed on the starboard side of the vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-240.explanation: Regardless of a vessel's own direction of travel, red buoys always mark the right-hand side of the fairway with reference to the downstream direction. A vessel travelling upstream, however, sees that geographically right-hand side as being on its own left as it heads upstream, so the buoy must be passed on the vessel's port side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-241.question: A vessel is travelling upstream in the fairway. Ahead lies a green buoy. On which side of the fairway is this buoy, and on which side of the vessel must it be passed?

options.a: It is on the left side of the fairway and must be passed on the port side of the vessel.
options.b: It is on the right side of the fairway and must be passed on the starboard side of the vessel.
options.c: It is on the left side of the fairway and must be passed on the starboard side of the vessel.
options.d: It is on the right side of the fairway and must be passed on the port side of the vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-241.explanation: With reference to the downstream direction, green buoys mark the left-hand side of the fairway. A vessel travelling against the current, i.e. upstream, sees that geographically left-hand side as being on its own right as it heads upstream, so the green buoy must be passed on the vessel's starboard side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-242.question: What function do yellow buoys fitted with a radar reflector have in front of bridge piers?

options.a: Marking the height of the bridge piers.
options.b: Marking a shoal in the bridge area.
options.c: Marking a closed bridge passage.
options.d: Making the bridge piers visible on the radar screen.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-242.explanation: Yellow buoys with a radar reflector positioned in front of bridge piers make the piers clearly visible on the radar screen, since solid structures like bridge piers are not always clearly distinguishable on radar in darkness or reduced visibility. This allows the fairway between the piers to be safely identified even without visual contact.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-244.question: What does this panel sign mean at a bridge passage?

options.a: Prohibition of passage and closure of navigation.
options.b: A structure requiring protection.
options.c: Passage closed, but navigable for powered small craft.
options.d: Passage closed, but navigable for small craft without propulsion machinery.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-244.explanation: This circular prohibition sign at a bridge passage means that the passage is completely closed to all shipping, regardless of vessel size or type of propulsion. It is used, for example, during construction work, after accidents, or in the event of an acute hazard at the bridge.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-3.question: When is a vessel 'underway'?

options.a: When it is neither at anchor nor made fast to the shore nor making way over ground.
options.b: When it is neither at anchor nor made fast to the shore nor aground.
options.c: When it is neither aground nor at anchor nor restricted in its ability to manoeuvre or not under command.
options.d: When it is neither made fast to the shore nor at anchor nor making way through the water.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-3.explanation: By definition, a vessel is 'underway' when it is neither at anchor, nor made fast to the shore or bank, nor aground. This definition is independent of whether the vessel is actually moving; even a drifting vessel or one unable to manoeuvre with a stopped engine counts as underway as long as none of the three exclusion conditions applies.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-34.question: Why should a small vessel not approach a large vessel underway too closely?

options.a: Because it would otherwise be unable to give way to the large vessel underway.
options.b: Approaching too closely is a violation of the basic rules of conduct in traffic.
options.c: It can suffer seasickness from the vessel's bow or stern wave.
options.d: It can be capsized by the vessel's bow or stern wave, or drawn into collision with it by suction.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-34.explanation: Large vessels underway generate substantial bow and stern waves as well as suction along their hull. If a small boat approaches too closely, these waves can capsize it, or the suction can pull it into a collision with the larger hull.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-37.question: What dangers can arise when a small vessel is overtaken by a larger vessel?

options.a: The smaller vessel can be pushed off course by pile-up, suction or swell and collide or capsize, and be pushed strongly off course in shallow water.
options.b: The larger vessel can be pushed off course by wave formation and collide or broach, and run aground in shallow water.
options.c: The smaller vessel can be pushed off course by pile-up, suction or swell and collide or broach, and run aground in shallow water.
options.d: The larger vessel can be pushed off course by pile-up, suction or swell and collide or broach, and run aground in shallow water.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-37.explanation: When a small vessel is overtaken by a larger one, the pile-up of water, suction and swell generated by the larger vessel create considerable hydrodynamic forces. The small vessel can be pushed off course, collide, or broach as a result, and in shallow water there is the additional danger of running aground due to the intensified suction effect.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-39.question: How can you tell whether the anchor is holding?

options.a: If no jerking is felt when a hand is laid on the anchor chain or rope, and the anchor bearing does not change.
options.b: If no jerking is felt when a hand is laid on the anchor chain or rope, and the vessel is not swinging.
options.c: If no jerking is felt when a hand is laid on the anchor chain or rope, and the anchor bearing does change.
options.d: If the anchor chain or rope does not vibrate and the compass heading does not change.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-39.explanation: The anchor is holding securely if no jerking can be felt when a hand is placed on the taut anchor chain or rope, meaning the anchor is not dragging along the bottom. In addition, the anchor bearing taken to fixed landmarks must not change, since a constant bearing shows that the vessel is not moving relative to the ground.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-49.question: What must be observed when refuelling?

options.a: Close windows, do not operate any electrical switches, take precautions against fuel overflow, no naked flames.
options.b: Switch off the engine, do not operate any electrical switches, take precautions against fuel overflow, no naked flames.
options.c: Switch off the engine, have a fire extinguisher ready, take precautions against fuel overflow, no naked flames.
options.d: Put the engine in neutral idle, do not operate any electrical switches, take precautions against fuel overflow, no naked flames.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-49.explanation: When refuelling, the engine must be switched off and no electrical switches operated, since fuel vapours can be ignited by even a small spark. In addition, precautions must be taken against fuel overflow, and naked flames or smoking must be strictly avoided to prevent fire and explosion hazards.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-60.question: What precautions must be taken when leaving the vessel for an extended period?

options.a: Close all seacocks and switch off the main switch of the electrical system.
options.b: Leave the vessel seaworthy and inform the harbour master.
options.c: Close the day tank and drain the fuel filter.
options.d: Fill up the fuel and water tanks and charge the electrical system.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-60.explanation: When leaving the vessel for an extended period, all seacocks must be closed to prevent water ingress through leaking valves, hoses or hose clamps while no one is aboard to intervene. In addition, the main switch of the electrical system should be switched off to rule out fires caused by short circuits in the live wiring.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-67.question: How often must inflatable life-saving equipment be serviced?

options.a: Annually and after every use or drill.
options.b: Annually, each time before the start of the water sports season.
options.c: According to the manufacturer's specification, at least every 3 years.
options.d: According to the manufacturer's specification, at least every 2 years.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-67.explanation: Inflatable life-saving equipment such as automatically-inflating lifejackets or liferafts must be serviced by an authorised service station according to the manufacturer's specifications, but at least every two years. This checks the airtightness, the inflation mechanism and the gas cartridge, since material ageing can compromise reliable operation in an emergency.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-103.question: What is prohibited in canals?

options.a: Overtaking.
options.b: Turning.
options.c: Anchoring.
options.d: Meeting/passing.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-103.explanation: Anchoring is prohibited in canals because these waterways are usually narrow and offer only a limited fairway width. An anchored vessel would block the tight fairway and create a considerable collision risk for the rest of the traffic.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-106.question: How are anchors that day marked if they could obstruct shipping?

options.a: With a white buoy marker.
options.b: With a red buoy marker.
options.c: With a yellow buoy marker.
options.d: With a green buoy marker.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-106.explanation: Anchors that could obstruct shipping are marked by day with a yellow buoy marker so that other vessels can recognise the position of the anchor and its chain in good time and steer clear of it.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-117.question: What does a red light, or a red and a green light, mean in front of a lock?

options.a: Exit prohibited, opening of the lock is being prepared.
options.b: Entry prohibited, closing of the lock is being prepared.
options.c: Entry prohibited, opening of the lock is being prepared.
options.d: Exit prohibited, closing of the lock is being prepared.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-117.explanation: A red light alone, or a red and a green light together, in front of a lock indicate that entry is prohibited because the lock chamber is currently being prepared for the next locking operation, for example by opening the gates or adjusting the water level. Only a green light signals clearance to enter.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-118.question: In what order do vessels that are not small craft, and small craft that are to be locked through together, enter the lock?

options.a: Small craft enter after the vessels that are not small craft, and without being asked to by the lock supervisor.
options.b: Small craft enter before the vessels that are not small craft, and without being asked to by the lock supervisor.
options.c: Small craft enter before the vessels that are not small craft, and before being asked to by the lock supervisor.
options.d: Small craft enter only after the vessels that are not small craft, and only after being asked to by the lock supervisor.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-118.explanation: When locking through together, the vessels that are not small craft enter first, since they are generally less manoeuvrable and need more space. Small craft enter only afterwards, and only on instruction from the lock supervisor, so that entry proceeds in an orderly and safe manner.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-119.question: Several small craft are to be locked together from the upper level down to the lower level. What must be particularly watched when entering the lock and during the locking process?

options.a: The last small craft must enter far enough in that it cannot ground on the sill when the lock is emptied. The mooring lines must be handled so as to avoid impacts against lock walls, gates or other vessels, and to allow the lines to be safely paid out.
options.b: The first small craft must enter far enough in that it cannot ground on the sill when the lock is filled. The mooring lines must be handled so as to avoid impacts against lock walls, gates or other vessels, and to allow the lines to be safely paid out.
options.c: The first small craft must enter far enough in that it cannot ground on the sill when the lock is emptied. The mooring lines must be handled so as to avoid impacts against lock walls, gates or other vessels, and to allow the lines to be safely paid out.
options.d: The last small craft must enter far enough in that it cannot ground on the sill when the lock is filled. The mooring lines must be handled so as to avoid impacts against lock walls, gates or other vessels, and to allow the lines to be safely paid out.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-119.explanation: When several small craft are locked together from the upper to the lower level, the first (furthest-in) small craft must move in far enough that it cannot ground on the sill at the lock gate when the water level is lowered (the lock is emptied). In addition, mooring lines must be handled so that safe paying-out is possible as the water level drops, and so that impacts against lock walls, gates or other vessels are avoided.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-213.question: What must be done with waste of any kind that accumulates on board?

options.a: Collect it on board and only throw it overboard in closed containers.
options.b: Collect it on board. It can be handed in at any lock.
options.c: Collect it on board and set it down on land at a mooring place.
options.d: Collect it on board and dispose of it properly ashore in the appropriate waste collection containers.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-213.explanation: All waste that accumulates on board must be collected and must never be thrown into the water, since inland waterways and lakes are sensitive ecosystems and in some cases also drinking-water reservoirs. Waste must be disposed of ashore in the designated waste collection containers.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-245.question: Why is it prohibited to use car tyres as fenders when passing through a lock?

options.a: Car tyres leave black marks on the boat and the lock wall.
options.b: Car tyres are not buoyant and can cause considerable disruption in locks.
options.c: Car tyres are buoyant and can cause considerable disruption in the lock.
options.d: Car tyres create too much friction.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-245.explanation: Car tyres are prohibited as fenders when passing through a lock because they are not buoyant: if a tyre comes loose or goes underwater, it can get caught on the lock's bollards, recesses or gate mechanisms, seriously disrupting the locking process or even causing damage.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-254.question: What is meant by a 'bilge keeler'?

options.a: A yacht with two side centreboards.
options.b: A yacht with two keels one behind the other.
options.c: A yacht with two side (bilge) keels.
options.d: A yacht with a single lifting keel/centreboard.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-254.explanation: A 'bilge keeler' is a yacht fitted with two side keels, usually angled in a V-shape, instead of a single centreline keel, providing additional stability when standing upright out of the water.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-255.question: What is the advantage of a bilge keeler compared with other keelboats?

options.a: The keel can be raised.
options.b: It can dry out standing upright without difficulty.
options.c: Its draught is greater.
options.d: Its leeway is less than that of other keelboats.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-255.explanation: The advantage of a bilge keeler is that, thanks to its two side keels, it can dry out standing upright on the bottom without difficulty and without tipping over, making it particularly suitable for tidal waters with low water levels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-256.question: What is meant by a 'centreboard keelboat' (Kielschwertyacht)?

options.a: A yacht with a ballast keel and an additional centreboard.
options.b: A yacht with a shallow, fixed ballast keel and an additional retractable centreboard.
options.c: A yacht with a retractable ballast keel.
options.d: A yacht with two side keels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-256.explanation: A centreboard keelboat combines a shallow, fixed ballast keel providing weight stability and a shallow draught with an additional retractable centreboard that can be raised as needed and improves close-hauled sailing and course-keeping.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-257.question: How do a dinghy's self-bailers, which are located below the waterline, work?

options.a: Through the pressure difference between air and water pressure.
options.b: Gravity makes the water flow overboard.
options.c: Through the inertia possessed by the boat.
options.d: Through the suction created when the boat is moving through the water.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-257.explanation: A dinghy's self-bailers, positioned below the waterline, make use of the suction created at the bottom of the hull when the boat is moving through the water: this low-pressure effect draws the water standing in the cockpit outward. When the boat is stationary this effect disappears, which is why the bailers do not work then.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-258.question: What is meant by 'form stability'?

options.a: A vessel's ability to right itself automatically after capsizing.
options.b: A vessel's ability to keep its course when the tiller is released.
options.c: A vessel's ability to retain its hull shape over the years even under heavy stress.
options.d: A vessel's ability, through its hull shape, to counteract heeling.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-258.explanation: 'Form stability' refers to a vessel's ability to resist heeling purely through its wide, flat hull shape: as the hull tilts, the centre of buoyancy shifts towards the leeward side, generating a righting moment.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-259.question: What is meant by 'weight stability'?

options.a: A vessel's ability, through its deep-lying ballast, to counteract heeling.
options.b: The possibility of counteracting heeling through a heavy crew weight.
options.c: The possibility of reducing heeling through additional internal ballast.
options.d: A vessel's ability, through its hull shape, to counteract heeling.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-259.explanation: 'Weight stability' refers to a vessel's ability to resist heeling by means of heavy ballast fitted deep below the hull. The low-lying centre of gravity creates a pendulum-like righting moment that counteracts the wind pressure on the sails.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-260.question: Which boats are predominantly 'weight-stable'?

options.a: Keelboats are predominantly 'weight-stable'.
options.b: Catamarans are predominantly 'weight-stable'.
options.c: Dinghies are predominantly 'weight-stable'.
options.d: Trimarans are predominantly 'weight-stable'.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-260.explanation: Keelboats are predominantly weight-stable, since their stability is generated mainly by a deep, heavy ballast keel, in contrast to form-stable boats, whose stability results mainly from the shape of the hull.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-261.question: Which boats are predominantly 'form-stable'?

options.a: Keelboats are predominantly 'form-stable'.
options.b: Centreboard keelboats are predominantly 'form-stable'.
options.c: Dinghies are predominantly 'form-stable'.
options.d: Bilge keelers are predominantly 'form-stable'.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-261.explanation: Dinghies are predominantly form-stable, since they generally lack a heavy ballast keel and their stability results mainly from their wide, flat hull shape and from the crew hiking out or using a trapeze.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-262.question: How can the stability of a form-stable boat be increased in strong wind?

options.a: By transferring water ballast.
options.b: By extending so-called trim flaps or an additional centreboard.
options.c: By shifting internal ballast.
options.d: By hiking out or by using the trapeze rig.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-262.explanation: In form-stable boats, stability can be increased in strong wind by the crew hiking out over the gunwale or using the trapeze, since this uses the crew's body weight as an additional lever arm on the windward side to counteract heeling.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-263.question: How does the righting moment of a dinghy change as it heels?

options.a: It initially decreases and reaches a maximum when the centre of buoyancy and centre of gravity lie one above the other, after which the dinghy capsizes.
options.b: It initially decreases and reaches its minimum, until the centre of buoyancy and centre of gravity lie one above the other, after which the dinghy capsizes.
options.c: It initially increases up to a maximum, then decreases again until the centre of buoyancy and centre of gravity lie one above the other, after which the dinghy capsizes.
options.d: It initially decreases to a minimum, then increases again until the centre of buoyancy and centre of gravity lie one above the other, after which the dinghy capsizes.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-263.explanation: As a dinghy heels progressively, its righting moment first increases up to a maximum. It then decreases again until the centre of buoyancy and the centre of gravity lie exactly above one another; once this point is exceeded, the dinghy capsizes, since no righting moment remains.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-264.question: How does the righting moment of a keelboat change as heeling steadily increases?

options.a: It decreases until reaching the critical angle of 90 degrees.
options.b: It increases until reaching the critical angle, which lies at about 70 degrees.
options.c: It increases and, after passing its maximum, only reaches its critical angle above 90 degrees.
options.d: It decreases until 90 degrees of heel and then increases steadily.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-264.explanation: For a keelboat, the righting moment initially increases with growing heel and reaches its maximum at a relatively small angle. It then decreases again, but thanks to the deep-lying ballast keel it remains positive up to a very large heel angle, well above 90 degrees, allowing the yacht to right itself even from a severe knockdown.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-266.question: How can a tiller be reached and operated safely even when the boat is heeling?

options.a: By replacing the tiller with a wheel.
options.b: By using a tiller extension (hiking stick).
options.c: By adjusting the traveller.
options.d: By hiking out using the trapeze.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-266.explanation: A tiller extension (hiking stick) allows the crew to safely reach and operate the tiller even while hiking out or hanging in the trapeze for weight compensation, since the extension lets the tiller be reached well beyond the gunwale.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-267.question: Why should ropes on board always be properly coiled?

options.a: So that it stays clear and ready to run when needed.
options.b: So that it is not damaged by UV radiation.
options.c: So that its breaking strength is preserved.
options.d: So that it can dry and does not rot.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-267.explanation: Ropes on board should always be properly coiled so that they stay clear when needed, meaning they can run out immediately without tangling or knotting. Rope that has not been coiled can become tangled and jam at a critical moment.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-268.question: Why should halyards always be properly coiled?

options.a: So that they can dry and do not rot.
options.b: So that they are not damaged by UV radiation.
options.c: So that they cannot be mistaken for sheets.
options.d: So that they can be paid out quickly and safely when needed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-268.explanation: Halyards must always be properly coiled so that, when needed - for example to quickly lower the sails in an emergency - they can be paid out swiftly and safely without snagging or tangling.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-269.question: What are the corners of a sail called?

options.a: Forestay, lower shroud, backstay.
options.b: Head, tack, clew.
options.c: Head, tack, tip.
options.d: Luff, foot, leech.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-269.explanation: The three corners of a sail are called the head (top corner), the tack (forward lower corner) and the clew (aft lower corner, where the sheet is attached).

sportboot-binnen-elwis-270.question: What are the edges of a sail called?

options.a: Luff, foot, leech.
options.b: Head, tack, tip.
options.c: Forestay, lower shroud, backstay.
options.d: Head, tack, clew.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-270.explanation: The three edges of a sail are called the luff (forward edge), the foot (lower edge) and the leech (aft edge).

sportboot-binnen-elwis-272.question: What dangers can arise if sails are allowed to luff (flap) for an extended period?

options.a: Luffing makes the boat capsize in stronger wind.
options.b: Luffing causes damage to neighbouring boats moored alongside.
options.c: Luffing damages the fabric and can cause seams to split.
options.d: Luffing causes injuries to the crew.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-272.explanation: A luffing sail flaps constantly and uncontrollably, subjecting the fabric and especially the seams to heavy repeated stress. Over time this causes material fatigue, damaging the cloth and potentially causing seams to split open.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-273.question: Why must even small damage to the sails be repaired immediately?

options.a: Because it can then only be used in a flat calm.
options.b: Because moisture can penetrate into the sail.
options.c: Because it reduces the sail's drive/thrust.
options.d: Because under wind pressure it quickly turns into major damage.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-273.explanation: Even small damage to sails must be repaired immediately, because a small tear can grow very quickly under the high wind pressure experienced while sailing. What starts as a minor blemish can turn into major damage within a short time, jeopardising the sail's continued use.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-274.question: How can the direction of the true wind be recognised while underway?

options.a: By the direction clouds are moving.
options.b: By the telltales on the mainsail.
options.c: By flags or other indicators ashore.
options.d: By the national ensign at the stern.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-274.explanation: While underway, onboard instruments such as wind vanes or telltales only show the apparent wind, which is the combination of true wind and the wind of the boat's own motion. The direction of the true wind is instead recognised from stationary reference points, such as flags, smoke or other indicators ashore.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-275.question: What wind is indicated by wind vanes or telltales while underway?

options.a: The wind direction.
options.b: The apparent wind.
options.c: The true wind.
options.d: The wind of the boat's own motion.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-275.explanation: Wind vanes and telltales on board always indicate the apparent wind while underway, since this results from the vector sum of the true wind and the headwind created by the boat's own motion.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-276.question: When do the true wind and the apparent wind come from the same direction on a sailing boat?

options.a: On a close-hauled course.
options.b: On a run (dead downwind).
options.c: On a broad reach.
options.d: On a beam reach.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-276.explanation: On a sailing boat, the true wind and the apparent wind come from the same direction when the boat is sailing dead downwind, i.e. the wind is coming exactly from astern. In this case, the headwind created by the boat's own motion, which acts in the opposite direction, only changes the magnitude of the resulting wind, not its direction.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-277.question: Why is the apparent wind weaker than the true wind when sailing dead downwind?

options.a: Regardless of wind direction, the apparent wind is always weaker than the true wind.
options.b: The true wind is reduced by the opposing headwind created by the boat's own motion.
options.c: The true wind is slowed down by the headwind created by the boat's own motion.
options.d: The apparent wind is slowed down by the suction along the sail.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-277.explanation: The apparent wind is the vector sum of the true wind and the boat's own wind (the headwind created by the boat's motion through the water). On a dead-downwind course the boat travels in the same direction as the wind, so its own boat-speed wind opposes the true wind and reduces its effective strength – the apparent wind is therefore weaker than the true wind. The faster the boat sails, the more pronounced this effect becomes.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-278.question: Why is the apparent wind stronger than the true wind on a close-hauled course?

options.a: Because on this course the true wind and the boat's own headwind add together in direction and strength.
options.b: Because on this course a slot effect forms between jib and mainsail that accelerates the wind.
options.c: Because, regardless of wind direction, the apparent wind is always stronger than the true wind.
options.d: Because the true wind is stronger close-hauled than on a reach.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-278.explanation: On a close-hauled course the boat's own headwind comes from nearly the same direction as the true wind. Because both wind components add together as vectors, the resulting apparent wind is stronger than the true wind and also comes from further forward.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-279.question: A boat has reefed while sailing close-hauled. A boat of the same type coming towards it is sailing unreefed. How can this be explained?

options.a: Boats are more stable when the wind comes from further aft.
options.b: The apparent wind is stronger on close-hauled courses and weaker on reaching and running courses than the true wind.
options.c: The true wind piles up against the sail on a reaching course and is therefore weaker.
options.d: On a close-hauled course the wind streams along the aerofoil-shaped curved sail and is thereby accelerated.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-279.explanation: Although both boats are sailing in the same true wind, they are on different points of sail relative to it, so a different apparent wind strength acts on each. The boat sailing close-hauled experiences a stronger apparent wind (true wind plus the boat's own headwind add together) and therefore needs to reef, while the boat coming towards it on a broader point of sail experiences a considerably weaker apparent wind.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-280.question: Why does the apparent wind veer aft (free) when a gust hits on a close-hauled course?

options.a: Because the wind direction is influenced by the sail trim, the apparent wind also changes.
options.b: Because the boat's own headwind initially stays the same while the true wind increases, the resulting apparent wind shifts aft (frees).
options.c: Because the Coriolis force also changes the wind's direction as it strengthens.
options.d: Because the boat's trim automatically changes course when the wind increases.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-280.explanation: During a gust the true wind's strength increases while the boat's speed – and therefore its own headwind – does not change immediately. Since the headwind component of the apparent wind becomes relatively smaller, the resulting apparent wind direction shifts aft (frees, or 'veers').

sportboot-binnen-elwis-281.question: When a gust hits on a close-hauled course, the apparent wind frees (veers aft). What benefit can be gained from this when beating to windward?

options.a: Ease the sails slightly to convert the gust into heel.
options.b: A spinnaker can be set.
options.c: Luff up to gain extra pointing height.
options.d: Bear away to sail at maximum height.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-281.explanation: Because the apparent wind direction frees during a gust, the boat can luff up while keeping the same angle to the (now freer) apparent wind – gaining extra pointing height against the true wind without needing to re-trim the sails.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-282.question: How should the centreboard of a dinghy be set when running dead downwind, and why?

options.a: It should never be fully raised, since otherwise it can't be reached to right the dinghy after a capsize.
options.b: It should be lowered. This makes the boat more stable and reduces the risk of capsizing during an accidental gybe.
options.c: It should be fully raised in strong winds to improve the dinghy's steerability.
options.d: It should be raised. This reduces drag but also the risk of capsizing during an accidental gybe.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-282.explanation: Running dead downwind, the sideways force of the wind barely acts on the hull, so a fully lowered centreboard only creates unnecessary drag through the water. In addition, a raised centreboard shortens the underwater lever arm, so the boat heels (and capsizes) less violently if an accidental gybe occurs.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-283.question: How do leeway and heel change if the centreboard of a dinghy is raised slightly while close-hauled?

options.a: Leeway increases, heel increases.
options.b: Leeway decreases, the boat becomes faster due to lower water resistance.
options.c: Leeway decreases, heel decreases.
options.d: Leeway increases, heel decreases.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-283.explanation: A partially raised centreboard offers less lateral resistance to the sideways force of the wind, so the boat makes more leeway. At the same time the lever arm between the sail's centre of effort and the hull's centre of lateral resistance shortens, reducing the heeling moment and therefore the heel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-284.question: With what degree of heel should a dinghy normally be sailed, and why?

options.a: Slightly heeled to leeward, since otherwise the sails can easily back to windward.
options.b: As heeled to windward as possible, because this reduces leeway and weather helm.
options.c: As upright as possible, since otherwise leeway and weather helm (tendency to round up) increase.
options.d: As upright as possible, since otherwise leeway and lee helm (tendency to bear away) increase.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-284.explanation: As heel increases, the underwater hull shape becomes asymmetric, which makes the boat carry weather helm and increases leeway, because the sail's centre of effort and the hull's centre of lateral resistance shift sideways relative to each other. A dinghy sailed as upright as possible is therefore faster and easier to steer.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-286.question: How does a jib sheet lead (car) that is too far forward affect the shape and load on the headsail?

options.a: The luff luffs (flutters), the foot is over-tensioned.
options.b: The luff luffs (flutters), the leech is over-tensioned.
options.c: The leech luffs (flutters), the luff is over-tensioned.
options.d: The foot luffs (flutters), the leech is over-tensioned.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-286.explanation: If the sheet lead is too far forward, the sheet pulls the sail more downward than aft, so the leech is over-tightened (closes up at the top) while the lower part of the sail – the foot – is not tensioned enough and flutters (luffs).

sportboot-binnen-elwis-287.question: How does a jib sheet lead (car) that is too far aft affect the shape and load on the headsail?

options.a: The foot luffs (flutters), the leech is over-tensioned.
options.b: The leech luffs (flutters), the luff is over-tensioned.
options.c: The luff luffs (flutters), the foot is over-tensioned.
options.d: The leech luffs (flutters), the foot is over-tensioned.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-287.explanation: If the sheet lead is too far aft, the sheet pulls the sail mainly aft rather than downward, so the leech stays too open and flutters (luffs), while the foot is over-tensioned.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-288.question: How should a sail be trimmed in light wind?

options.a: The sheets must be hauled in hard.
options.b: The sail should have a deep, full shape.
options.c: The sail should be trimmed flat.
options.d: The sheets must be eased.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-288.explanation: In light wind, a sail trimmed with a deep, full curvature generates more drive, since the airflow is guided over a larger curved surface, allowing useful power to be extracted even from weak wind.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-289.question: How should a sail be trimmed in strong wind?

options.a: The sheets must be eased.
options.b: The sheets must be hauled in hard.
options.c: The sail should be trimmed flat.
options.d: It should be trimmed with a deep, full shape.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-289.explanation: In strong wind the sail is trimmed flat to reduce drive, lower the angle of attack, and thereby avoid excessive heel and rudder load; a flat sail generates less power and lets the wind spill more easily.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-290.question: How does an outhaul influence the trim of the sail?

options.a: Depending on tension, the lower part of the headsail becomes fuller or flatter.
options.b: Depending on tension, the aft part of the mainsail becomes fuller or flatter.
options.c: Depending on tension, the aft part of the headsail becomes fuller or flatter.
options.d: Depending on tension, the lower part of the mainsail becomes fuller or flatter.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-290.explanation: The outhaul tensions the foot of the mainsail along the boom. The harder it is pulled in, the flatter the lower third of the sail becomes; when eased, the sail becomes fuller in that area.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-291.question: To hold a dinghy on course while close-hauled, the tiller must constantly be pulled away from the side the sails are on. How can this trim fault be corrected?

options.a: Trim the headsail flatter; shift crew weight aft.
options.b: Trim the mainsail flatter; shift crew weight aft.
options.c: Trim the mainsail flatter; shift crew weight forward.
options.d: Trim the headsail flatter; shift crew weight forward.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-291.explanation: If the tiller must constantly be held away from the sails, the boat is carrying weather helm – usually caused by a mainsail trimmed too full and too aft-loaded, and/or excessive heel. The fix is to trim the mainsail flatter and shift crew weight aft, easing the bow and reducing heel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-292.question: To hold a dinghy on course while close-hauled, the tiller must constantly be pushed towards the side the sails are on. How can this trim fault be corrected?

options.a: Trim the mainsail flatter, shift crew weight aft.
options.b: Trim the mainsail fuller, shift crew weight aft.
options.c: Trim the mainsail flatter, shift crew weight forward.
options.d: Trim the mainsail fuller, shift crew weight forward.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-292.explanation: If the tiller must constantly be pushed towards the sails, the boat is carrying lee helm – it tends to bear away from the wind. The fix is to trim the mainsail fuller, generating more drive aft, and shift crew weight forward to bury the bow slightly and unload the stern.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-294.question: What influence does increasing heel have on the trim of the boat?

options.a: Weather helm (tendency to round up into the wind) increases.
options.b: Lee helm (tendency to bear away) increases.
options.c: None.
options.d: Weather helm increases up to about 45° of heel, then decreases again.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-294.explanation: As heel increases, the leeward half of the hull sinks deeper and more asymmetrically into the water than the windward side. This causes the underwater hull shape to generate a turning tendency towards the wind about the vertical axis – so the boat carries weather helm and wants to round up.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-295.question: Which manoeuvres did the boat perform at points 1, 2 and 3 on the marked course?

options.a: 1 crash gybe (Q-turn), 2 gybe, 3 tack.
options.b: 1 tack, 2 crash gybe (Q-turn), 3 gybe.
options.c: 1 gybe, 2 tack, 3 crash gybe (Q-turn).
options.d: 1 tack, 2 gybe, 3 crash gybe (Q-turn).

sportboot-binnen-elwis-295.explanation: Without the accompanying diagram, the assignment can only be reasoned out from the definitions: in a tack the boat turns its bow through the wind, in a gybe it turns its stern through the wind, and a crash gybe/tack (Q-Wende) is an unintended, usually uncontrolled gybe or tack caused by a helming error. The sequence of direction changes shown on the marked course corresponds to these three manoeuvre types in that order.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-296.question: What should be done with the centreboard and rudder of a dinghy when the boat is left on a mooring buoy?

options.a: Lower the centreboard and rudder so the boat can swing freely.
options.b: Raise the centreboard, lower the rudder, so the boat can swing freely.
options.c: Lower the centreboard, raise the rudder, so the boat can swing freely.
options.d: Raise the centreboard and rudder blade, so the boat can swing freely.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-296.explanation: If the centreboard and rudder blade are left down, they act like anchoring points in the water and prevent the boat from swinging freely around the mooring buoy as wind or current change, which can cause unnecessary yawing or damage. Raising both allows the boat to align itself freely around the buoy.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-298.question: A sailboat is sailing close-hauled when the windward shroud suddenly breaks. Which manoeuvre is appropriate?

options.a: Crash gybe (Q-turn).
options.b: Tack.
options.c: Heave-to / round up head to wind.
options.d: Gybe.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-298.explanation: If the windward shroud breaks, the mast is no longer supported on that side, and continuing close-hauled would overload it through the sail's driving forces and could bring it down. By tacking, the broken shroud ends up on the now-unloaded leeward side, so the mast is barely loaded while crossing head to wind, and afterwards it is again held by the intact shroud, now on the new windward side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-299.question: A sailboat is sailing close-hauled under mainsail alone in strong wind. Suddenly the forestay breaks. What must be done immediately?

options.a: Round up head to wind.
options.b: Sheet in hard and luff up.
options.c: Gybe.
options.d: Bear away onto a dead-downwind course.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-299.explanation: Without the forestay, the mast loses its forward support; the driving force of a sheeted-in mainsail on a close-hauled course would push the mast forward beyond its limits and could break it. Bearing away immediately onto a run unloads the mainsail, minimises the forward load on the mast, and thereby temporarily secures it.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-300.question: A sailboat is sailing close-hauled under mainsail alone in strong wind and the forestay breaks. What can be used to quickly rig a makeshift replacement for the broken forestay?

options.a: The bow or stern mooring line.
options.b: The jib sheet or the main halyard.
options.c: The jib sheet or a reefing line.
options.d: The jib or a halyard.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-300.explanation: In this emergency, the jib itself (still bent on, run up and secured to the bow) or a spare halyard led from the masthead to the bow and made fast can be used to provisionally take over the forestay's function and support the mast forward until a harbour is reached.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-43.question: What must be done if fuel or oil gets into the bilge?

options.a: Spread it evenly.
options.b: Soak it up with rags and dispose of it in an environmentally sound way.
options.c: Ventilate the compartment and wait.
options.d: Neutralise it with an appropriate agent.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-43.explanation: Fuel and oil must never be pumped out into the water via the bilge pump, since this violates water protection rules and can cause serious environmental damage. Contamination must therefore be soaked up with rags, oil-absorbent material or similar and disposed of properly as hazardous waste.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-1.question: What must be done if it is not clear before the start of the voyage who is skipper?

options.a: A holder of a boating licence must take on the responsibility.
options.b: The responsible skipper must be determined.
options.c: A holder of a boating licence must take command of the vessel.
options.d: The responsible skipper must be elected.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-1.explanation: Under inland waterway navigation rules, every vessel must have a clearly designated responsible skipper who is liable for safe navigation and compliance with the regulations. If this is not settled before departure, those on board must expressly determine who takes on this responsibility – there is no provision for an election or an automatic assignment to whoever holds a boating licence.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-2.question: In which cases may a person neither operate a recreational boat nor independently determine its course or speed?

options.a: If impaired in safe operation due to physical or mental defects, or the consumption of alcoholic drinks or other intoxicants, or if a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5 ‰ or more is present in the body.
options.b: …or if a blood alcohol concentration of 0.8 ‰ or more is present in the body.
options.c: …or if a blood alcohol concentration of 0.3 ‰ or more is present in the body.
options.d: …or if a blood alcohol concentration of 1.0 ‰ or more is present in the body.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-2.explanation: On inland waterways, the fitness-to-operate limit for recreational boat operators is a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5 per mille; from this level onward, impairment is assumed regardless of any actually observable symptoms. In addition, and irrespective of the blood alcohol level, anyone who is noticeably impaired in safe operation by alcohol, other intoxicants, or physical or mental defects is excluded from operating the vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-4.question: How long does a short blast (

options.a: About 1 second.
options.b: About 2 seconds.
options.c: Less than 4 seconds.
options.d: Less than 1 second.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-4.explanation: Under the internationally standardised sound signal rules, a short blast lasts about one second, while a long blast lasts considerably longer. This defined duration underlies all sound signals (e.g. when turning, overtaking, or in restricted visibility) and must be given so that it is clearly distinguishable.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-5.question: How long does a long blast (

options.a: About 4 - 6 seconds.
options.b: About 2 - 6 seconds.
options.c: About 1 - 2 seconds.
options.d: About 6 - 8 seconds.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-5.explanation: Under the sound signal rules, a long blast lasts about 4 to 6 seconds, clearly distinguishing it from the short, roughly one-second blast. This clear time distinction ensures that sound signals, for example when announcing a course change, can be unambiguously recognised.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-6.question: When is a vessel under sail regarded as a power-driven vessel?

options.a: When it is under way using engine power at the same time.
options.b: When it makes no way through the water while sailing.
options.c: When it makes no way over ground while sailing.
options.d: When it is fitted with a propulsion engine.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-6.explanation: As soon as a sailing vessel also uses its engine in addition to its set sails, it is legally regarded as a power-driven vessel and must display the appropriate shape (cone) and apply the right-of-way rules for power-driven vessels – the priority that vessels under sail alone enjoy over power-driven vessels no longer applies.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-8.question: Which side is called the windward side?

options.a: The side facing the wind.
options.b: The side to the right of the direction of travel.
options.c: The side away from the wind.
options.d: The side to the left of the direction of travel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-8.explanation: Windward always refers to the side of a vessel that faces the wind, regardless of the direction of travel. This definition is important for applying the right-of-way rules between sailing vessels, where the position relative to the wind is, among other things, decisive for priority.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-9.question: Which side is called the leeward side?

options.a: The side to the left of the direction of travel.
options.b: The side away from the wind.
options.c: The side to the right of the direction of travel.
options.d: The side facing the wind.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-9.explanation: Leeward is the opposite of windward and refers to the side of a vessel facing away from the wind. The distinction between windward and leeward underlies the right-of-way rules between sailing vessels as well as behaviour when berthing, casting off, and anchoring.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-12.question: What kind of lantern may a sailing vessel of less than 20 m in length carry instead of the sidelights and sternlight?

options.a: A two-colour lantern at or near the masthead.
options.b: A two-colour lantern at a clearly visible position.
options.c: A tricolour lantern at or near the masthead.
options.d: A tricolour lantern at a clearly visible position.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-12.explanation: Sailing vessels under 20 m in length may carry a combined tricolour lantern (red/green/white) at or near the masthead instead of separate sidelights and a sternlight. This simplified lighting is well visible and adequate as long as the vessel is sailing under sail alone.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-14.question: How do two power boats approaching each other on reciprocal (head-on) courses give way?

options.a: The windward vessel must give way to the leeward vessel.
options.b: The leeward vessel must give way to the windward vessel.
options.c: Each vessel must alter its course to starboard.
options.d: Each vessel must alter its course to port.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-14.explanation: In a direct or near-direct head-on encounter between two power-driven vessels, the rule 'starboard to starboard' applies: both vessels alter course to starboard, so they pass port side to port side. This corresponds to the internationally standard give-way rule for power vessels meeting head-on.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-15.question: Two power boats approach on crossing courses. There is a risk of collision. Who must give way?

options.a: The vessel that has the other on its starboard side must give way.
options.b: The vessel that has the other on its port side must give way.
options.c: The leeward vessel must give way to the windward vessel.
options.d: The windward vessel must give way to the leeward vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-15.explanation: On crossing courses between two power-driven vessels, the give-way rules require that the vessel which has the other on its starboard side must give way – similar to a right-of-way-from-the-right rule in road traffic. The other vessel has right of way accordingly and must maintain its course and speed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-31.question: Which leaflet contains guidance on behaviour to protect rare animals and plants and to keep waterways clean?

options.a: The 10 golden rules for water sports enthusiasts.
options.b: The 15 rules of conduct for water sports enthusiasts.
options.c: The 15 golden rules for water sports enthusiasts.
options.d: The 10 basic rules for water sports enthusiasts.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-31.explanation: The '10 golden rules for water sports enthusiasts' is a well-known leaflet issued by nature conservation organisations and waterway authorities that summarises practical behaviour recommendations for recreational boaters to protect plant and animal life and to keep the waterways clean.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-32.question: How can one help preserve and promote living conditions for plant and animal life in waterways and wetlands?

options.a: Through environmentally conscious behaviour and observing the "Ten golden rules for the conduct of water sports enthusiasts in nature".
options.b: Through environmentally conscious behaviour and observing the "Ten basic rules for water sports".
options.c: Through careful conduct and observing the traffic regulations.
options.d: Through foresighted navigation and giving way in accordance with the traffic regulations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-32.explanation: The 'Ten golden rules' summarise concrete behaviours, such as avoiding reed beds, breeding and resting sites, and shallow-water zones. A water sports enthusiast who consciously follows these recommendations actively helps preserve sensitive shoreline habitats and the species living there.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-33.question: Why should reed beds and densely vegetated shoreline zones be given as wide a berth as possible?

options.a: Because the propeller could be blocked by the plants.
options.b: Because these zones are frequently resting and breeding sites for especially protection-worthy birds, or fish spawning grounds.
options.c: Because there is a risk of running aground in these zones.
options.d: Because swimmers are hard to spot in these zones.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-33.explanation: Reed beds and densely vegetated shoreline zones provide refuge, breeding and feeding areas for waterbirds, and serve as spawning grounds for many fish species. Wash, noise, and boat traffic through these zones significantly disturb these sensitive habitats, which is why a sufficient safety distance must be maintained.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-35.question: Why should one approach and berth against the current and wind whenever possible?

options.a: Because this increases the steering effect of the propeller.
options.b: Because this avoids suction effects and wash.
options.c: Because this compensates for the effects of waves and water depth.
options.d: Because the vessel can be manoeuvred more safely this way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-35.explanation: Approaching against current and wind keeps the vessel more responsive to the helm, because sufficient flow over the rudder is maintained even at low speed over ground, and the boat behaves more predictably when stopping. Berthing with current or wind from astern, by contrast, would make manoeuvring considerably more difficult and less predictable.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-38.question: Where can you find information about environmentally friendly paints, varnishes and antifouling coatings for your boat?

options.a: From the Federal Environment Agency (Umweltbundesamt).
options.b: In the Recreational Craft Charter Regulation.
options.c: In the Recreational Craft Licence Regulation.
options.d: From the Federal Ministry for Digital and Transport.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-38.explanation: The Federal Environment Agency (Umweltbundesamt) is the responsible authority that provides information and recommendations on environmentally sound boat paints, varnishes and antifouling coatings, since these products can contain pollutants that enter the water and harm aquatic organisms.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-40.question: What is the most favourable angle of approach when berthing?

options.a: An angle of 90° to 100°.
options.b: As acute an angle as possible.
options.c: An angle of 60° to 70°.
options.d: As obtuse an angle as possible.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-40.explanation: An acute angle of approach to a pier or jetty allows a gentle, controlled approach with a low sideways closing speed, leaving enough time and margin to counter-steer with rudder and engine and avoid a hard impact.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-41.question: How does a vessel generally behave in reverse gear with a right-hand (clockwise) turning propeller?

options.a: The stern swings to port.
options.b: The stern swings to starboard.
options.c: The bow swings to port.
options.d: The vessel's heading does not change.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-41.explanation: In reverse, the paddlewheel (transverse thrust) effect of a propeller that turns clockwise when going ahead effectively reverses, causing it to pull the stern to port when going astern. This effect must be taken into account when manoeuvring in reverse, for example when casting off.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-42.question: What does the kill cord (quick-stop / dead man's switch) do?

options.a: It interrupts the ignition circuit or fuel supply.
options.b: It briefly interrupts the engine's running.
options.c: It automatically starts the engine.
options.d: It automatically reverses thrust.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-42.explanation: The kill cord (dead man's switch), when pulled, immediately interrupts the ignition circuit or fuel supply and thereby stops the engine – for example if the helmsman falls overboard. This prevents an unmanned boat from continuing to run out of control and endangering people in the water.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-44.question: What is meant by a right-hand (clockwise) turning propeller?

options.a: Viewed from ahead, going ahead, the propeller turns clockwise.
options.b: Viewed from astern, going ahead, the propeller turns clockwise.
options.c: Viewed from astern, going ahead, the propeller turns counter-clockwise.
options.d: Viewed from ahead, going astern, the propeller turns counter-clockwise.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-44.explanation: A propeller's direction of rotation is, by definition, observed from astern (looking forward from the stern) while going ahead. If the propeller turns clockwise under these conditions, it is called a right-hand (or clockwise) turning propeller.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-45.question: What is meant by a left-hand (counter-clockwise) turning propeller?

options.a: Viewed from astern, going ahead, the propeller turns clockwise.
options.b: Viewed from ahead, going astern, the propeller turns clockwise.
options.c: Viewed from ahead, going ahead, the propeller turns counter-clockwise.
options.d: Viewed from astern, going ahead, the propeller turns counter-clockwise.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-45.explanation: Analogous to the definition of a right-hand turning propeller, this is also observed from astern while going ahead: if the propeller turns counter-clockwise under these conditions, it is a left-hand (counter-clockwise) turning propeller.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-46.question: What is meant by the indirect steering effect (paddlewheel/transverse thrust effect) of the propeller?

options.a: The sideways displacement of the stern.
options.b: The sideways displacement of the bow.
options.c: Displacement to the rear.
options.d: Displacement to the front.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-46.explanation: The paddlewheel (transverse thrust) effect arises from the uneven flow into the propeller and from the propeller's slipstream striking the rudder or hull at an angle. This displaces the stern sideways, an effect especially noticeable at low speed and in reverse, which can be used deliberately when manoeuvring.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-47.question: Why is it important to know the direction of propeller rotation?

options.a: It helps when overtaking.
options.b: It helps in holding a course.
options.c: It helps when manoeuvring.
options.d: It helps when meeting other vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-47.explanation: The direction of propeller rotation determines which way the paddlewheel (transverse thrust) effect displaces the stern. Knowing this direction lets a skipper use it deliberately when berthing, casting off, and turning in confined spaces to manoeuvre the vessel more precisely.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-48.question: Which side is recommended for berthing with a right-hand turning propeller, and why?

options.a: The starboard side – the transverse thrust effect pulls the vessel towards the pier.
options.b: The port side – the transverse thrust effect pulls the vessel towards the pier.
options.c: Either the starboard or port side, depending on the rudder position.
options.d: There is no recommended side for berthing.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-48.explanation: With a right-hand turning propeller, the transverse thrust effect in reverse gear (used to brake when berthing) pulls the stern to port. Berthing on the port side therefore means this effect pulls the stern, and hence the vessel, towards the pier, making the berthing manoeuvre easier.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-50.question: On a vessel with an outboard motor and no separate rudder, how is the steering effect achieved?

options.a: Through the propeller slipstream and the direction the propeller is pointed.
options.b: Through propeller drag and the propeller's angle of attack.
options.c: Through propeller drag and the direction the propeller is pointed.
options.d: Through the propeller slipstream and the propeller's angle of attack.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-50.explanation: Since an outboard motor without a separate rudder is swung together with the propeller, the steering effect comes from the directed propeller slipstream, which is aimed in the desired direction as the whole motor is turned, moving the stern accordingly.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-51.question: Why does the steering effect on a vessel with an inboard engine and fixed shaft take relatively long to develop after going astern?

options.a: Because the transverse thrust effect creates suction at the propeller.
options.b: Because it only begins once the rudder blade is being flowed over by water.
options.c: Because the transverse thrust effect creates suction at the rudder.
options.d: Because of the distance between the propeller and the rudder blade.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-51.explanation: With a fixed shaft and a separate rudder, the rudder only has effect once water is flowing purposefully over the rudder blade. When switching to reverse, sufficient propeller wash/flow onto the rudder blade must first build up, which is why steering effect initially takes a while to develop.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-52.question: The engine should be monitored continuously while under way. What must be watched particularly closely?

options.a: Injection pump pressure, impeller pump, oil pump.
options.b: Cooling water discharge, rev counter, drive belt tension.
options.c: Engine temperature, oil pressure, charge indicator light.
options.d: Propeller RPM, gearbox oil temperature, oil pressure.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-52.explanation: Engine temperature, oil pressure and the charge (alternator) warning light are the key parameters to monitor, since deviations here provide an early warning of dangerous faults such as loss of cooling water, lubrication failure, or a defective electrical charging system, before major engine damage occurs.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-53.question: The temperature of the propulsion engine exceeds the permitted limits. What could the possible cause be?

options.a: Defective thermostat, defective clutch, closed seacock, coolant level too low.
options.b: Defective thermostat, defective impeller pump, closed seacock, battery voltage too high.
options.c: Defective thermostat, defective impeller pump, closed seacock, coolant level too low.
options.d: Too much engine oil, defective impeller pump, closed seacock, coolant level too low.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-53.explanation: Engine overheating is caused almost always by a fault in the cooling water circuit: a defective thermostat no longer regulates coolant flow correctly, a defective impeller pump delivers no or too little cooling water, a closed seacock cuts off the water supply entirely, and too low a coolant level results in inadequate cooling.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-54.question: The charge warning lamp does not go out after starting. What could the possible cause be?

options.a: Broken drive belt and high power consumption.
options.b: Alternator or alternator regulator defective.
options.c: The starter motor has failed after starting.
options.d: Engine RPM too high.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-54.explanation: The charge warning lamp shows whether the alternator is charging the battery; if it does not go out after starting, no charging current is being generated. The most common causes are a defective alternator or a defective regulator that is not controlling the charging voltage correctly.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-55.question: The oil warning light stays on after starting. What could the possible cause be?

options.a: Too much engine oil in the engine.
options.b: Pressure switch or oil pump defective.
options.c: Engine RPM too high.
options.d: RCD (residual current device) defective.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-55.explanation: The oil warning light signals inadequate lubrication oil pressure. If it stays on after starting, this usually points to a defective oil pressure switch or a failed oil pump – in this case the engine should be shut down immediately to prevent engine damage from lack of lubrication.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-56.question: The engine has been started. What could be the cause if the engine stalls right after engaging the drive shaft?

options.a: Clogged oil filter.
options.b: Clogged air filter.
options.c: Blocked propeller.
options.d: Blocked fuel supply.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-56.explanation: If the engine stalls exactly when the clutch is engaged, this points to excessive mechanical resistance on the drive shaft, for example a blocked propeller (e.g. fouled by lines, net debris, or having struck the bottom), which suddenly increases the load on the engine and stalls it.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-57.question: An outboard motor with a full tank stops while running. What could be the causes?

options.a: Vent screw closed; blocked fuel line.
options.b: Intake nozzles too large or too small.
options.c: Fuel tank cap is open.
options.d: Propeller shaft screw is loose.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-57.explanation: The tank's vent screw must be open while running so outside air can flow in; if it is closed, a vacuum forms in the tank and cuts off fuel flow to the engine. Likewise, a blocked fuel line stops fuel reaching the engine even though the tank is full, causing it to die. Both are classic, easily fixed fault sources on outboard motors that every powerboat operator should recognize.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-58.question: Which publications contain important rules and tips for water sports enthusiasts, equipment recommendations for pleasure craft, and guidance on environmentally responsible behavior on the water?

options.a: Nautical publications such as "Sicherheit auf dem Wasser" and the International Code of Signals.
options.b: Nautical publications such as "Sicherheit auf dem Wasser" and "Sicher auf See".
options.c: International Code of Signals and the Ordinance on the Safety of Sea Navigation.
options.d: Ordinance on the Safety of Sea Navigation and nautical publications such as "Sicher auf See".

sportboot-binnen-elwis-58.explanation: The nautical publications "Sicherheit auf dem Wasser" and "Sicher auf See", issued by the German Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH), are aimed specifically at water sports enthusiasts and contain practical rules, equipment recommendations, and environmental guidance. They supplement the official regulations with practical safety tips but are not themselves legal regulations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-61.question: How should a narrow waterway be navigated when approaching vessels moored along the bank?

options.a: Reduce speed to avoid harmful suction and wash.
options.b: Reduce speed and, if necessary, depart from the keep-right rule.
options.c: Maintain speed so that planing avoids harmful suction and wash.
options.d: Stop alongside the moored vessels and check that no third party is being obstructed or harmed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-61.explanation: When passing moored vessels in narrow waterways, speed must be reduced so that suction and wash do not damage the moored boats or facilities and no one is endangered. This follows from the general duty of care, under which every vessel operator must take all precautions required by the circumstances to avoid damage to vessels, installations, or banks.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-62.question: Where should the gas cylinders of a liquid gas (LPG) installation be stored?

options.a: Preferably on deck, protected from sunlight, otherwise in a specially enclosed compartment for gas cylinders that is ventilated at the top.
options.b: Preferably in the forepeak, protected from sunlight, otherwise in a specially enclosed compartment for gas cylinders with an opening to the outside at floor level.
options.c: Preferably on deck, protected from sunlight, otherwise in a specially enclosed compartment for gas cylinders with an opening to the outside at floor level.
options.d: Preferably low down in the vessel, protected from sunlight, otherwise in a specially enclosed compartment for gas cylinders with an opening to the outside at floor level.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-62.explanation: LPG cylinders should preferably be stored on deck, shielded from direct sunlight. If that is not possible, they belong in a dedicated, enclosed gas locker with an opening at floor level leading directly overboard, so that any leaking gas — heavier than air — drains straight over the side instead of collecting inside the hull.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-63.question: Why are the liquid gases propane and butane particularly dangerous on board?

options.a: Both gases are heavier than water and form an explosive mixture with water.
options.b: Both gases are heavier than air and form an explosive mixture with water.
options.c: Both gases are heavier than air and form an explosive mixture with air.
options.d: Both gases are lighter than air and form an explosive mixture with air.
