sportboot-binnen-elwis-63.explanation: Propane and butane are heavier than air, so if they leak they sink and collect in the bilge, where they cannot escape on their own. Mixed with air within a certain concentration range they form a highly explosive mixture that can be ignited by even a small spark.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-64.question: What must be done if liquid gas gets into the interior of the boat?

options.a: Shut off the gas supply and provide ventilation. Also do not operate any electrical switches and call for help by telephone.
options.b: Empty the gas line and provide ventilation. Also do not operate any electrical switches and do not use any telephones.
options.c: Empty the gas line and check for gas-free air with a lighter, and call for help by radio or mobile phone.
options.d: Shut off the gas supply and provide ventilation. Also do not operate any electrical switches and do not use any radio or mobile phones.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-64.explanation: If liquid gas gets into the boat's interior, the gas supply (main valve) must first be shut off and good ventilation provided so the gas can dissipate. Electrical switches, radios, and mobile phones must never be operated or used, since even a small spark can ignite the gas-air mixture.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-65.question: What must be checked before putting a liquid gas installation into operation?

options.a: The installation must have been inspected and approved and be checked annually. It may only be commissioned by a specially certified person.
options.b: The inspection and approval of the installation must not be more than three years old. The main valve and other shut-off valves must be opened.
options.c: The installation must have been inspected and approved; it may only be commissioned by a specially certified person.
options.d: The installation must have been inspected and approved, and lines and connections must be leak-tight. The main valve and other shut-off valves must be opened.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-65.explanation: Before commissioning, the LPG installation must have been approved by a qualified inspector, and all lines and connections must be checked for leak-tightness; only then are the main valve and the other shut-off valves opened. This is the only way to ensure that no gas can escape uncontrolled.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-66.question: What must be observed when a liquid gas installation is taken out of service?

options.a: The gas cylinder must be completely emptied.
options.b: The main valve and shut-off valves must be closed.
options.c: The gas cylinder must be disposed of properly.
options.d: The installation must be made gas-free.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-66.explanation: When an LPG installation is taken out of service, the main valve on the cylinder and all further shut-off valves in the line must be closed. This prevents gas from continuing to escape through an unnoticed leak in the line while the installation is unattended.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-68.question: Which type of fire extinguisher is suitable for pleasure craft, and how often must a fire extinguisher be inspected?

options.a: CO2 extinguisher, at least every 2 years.
options.b: ABC powder extinguisher, at least once a year.
options.c: ABC powder and foam extinguishers, at least every 2 years.
options.d: Foam extinguisher, at least once a year.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-68.explanation: ABC powder and foam extinguishers are suitable for pleasure craft, as they are effective against the fire classes typically found on board (solids, liquids, and to some extent gases). Fire extinguishers must be inspected for functionality by a qualified person at least every two years.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-69.question: What measures must be taken to effectively fight a fire with a fire extinguisher?

options.a: Read the instructions and use the extinguisher immediately, fighting the fire from below if possible.
options.b: Ensure smoke can escape and use the extinguisher in good time, aiming the extinguishing jet directly into the flames.
options.c: Cut off the air supply, use the extinguisher only once at the seat of the fire, and fight the fire from below if possible.
options.d: Cut off the air supply and use the extinguisher with sparing bursts, fighting the fire from above if possible.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-69.explanation: To fight a fire effectively, the air supply to the fire must first be cut off, the extinguisher should only be deployed once directly at the seat of the fire so as not to waste its limited capacity, and the fire should be attacked from below, at the base of the flames, wherever possible.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-70.question: How must one behave after a collision?

options.a: Render assistance and remain at the scene until no further assistance is needed; give a distress signal.
options.b: Render assistance and remain at the scene until no further assistance is needed; notify the water police.
options.c: Render assistance and remain at the scene until no further assistance is needed; restore watertight closure.
options.d: Render assistance and remain at the scene until no further assistance is needed; exchange all necessary information.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-70.explanation: After a collision, everyone involved must render assistance and stay at the scene until no further assistance is needed. In addition, all necessary details must be exchanged (name, address, vessel data, insurance) so that claims can be settled and the accident properly documented.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-71.question: What factors are mainly decisive for weather phenomena, i.e. for wind and precipitation?

options.a: Air pressure change, solar radiation, and altitude.
options.b: Air pressure change, humidity, and temperature.
options.c: Air pressure change, time of day, and temperature.
options.d: Air pressure change, humidity, and season.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-71.explanation: Wind and precipitation are essentially created by air pressure differences, which generate compensating currents (wind), and by humidity and temperature, which determine whether and how much water vapor condenses and falls as precipitation. These three factors are central to every weather forecast.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-72.question: In what situation may distress signals be given?

options.a: When there is danger to the life or limb of persons, or the vessel can no longer be safely maneuvered.
options.b: When there is danger to the life or limb of persons or to significant property, and help is therefore needed.
options.c: When there is danger to the life or limb of persons, and help is therefore needed.
options.d: When there is danger to the life or limb of persons, to significant property, or to the marine environment.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-72.explanation: Distress signals may only be given when there is genuine danger to the life or limb of persons and help is therefore needed as a result. Misusing them for mere property damage or without a genuine emergency is prohibited, since it ties up and endangers real rescue operations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-76.question: What does the general duty of care encompass?

options.a: Endangering human life, damage to vessels, installations or banks, and harm to the environment.
options.b: Everything necessary must be done to avoid endangering human life, obstructing shipping, and harming the environment.
options.c: Avoidance of danger to human life, of damage to vessels, installations or banks, of obstruction to shipping, and of harm to the environment.
options.d: Everything necessary must be done to avoid damage to vessels, installations or banks, obstruction to shipping, and harm to the environment.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-76.explanation: The general duty of care requires every vessel operator, even without a specific individual rule, to take all precautions required by the circumstances. The aim is to avoid danger to human life, damage to vessels, installations, or banks, obstruction of shipping, and harm to the environment.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-77.question: Under what circumstances may the applicable rules on conduct in traffic on inland waterways be departed from?

options.a: In the case of an immediately impending danger to oneself or others.
options.b: When an encounter with another vessel is imminent.
options.c: In the case of an indirectly impending danger to oneself or others.
options.d: When an overtaking maneuver is imminent.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-77.explanation: Departure from the applicable traffic rules is permitted only when unavoidable to avert an immediately impending danger to oneself or others. This exception must be interpreted narrowly and does not justify routine deviation out of convenience.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-81.question: Where can one obtain information about traffic restrictions and current information on inland waterways?

options.a: From the Waterways and Shipping Administration, on the internet at www.elwis.de, and from the water police.
options.b: In Part II of the Inland Waterways Regulations (Binnenschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung).
options.c: From a water management office and from the water police.
options.d: In the Inland Vessel Inspection Ordinance.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-81.explanation: Up-to-date information on traffic restrictions, water levels, and closures on inland waterways is available from the federal Waterways and Shipping Administration (WSV), via the internet portal www.elwis.de, and from the water police. These bodies also publish shipping notices such as traffic reports and notices to inland navigation.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-84.question: Where can one find the general traffic rules for inland waterways and for the Rhine?

options.a: Inland Vessel Inspection Ordinance, Rhine Navigation Police Regulations.
options.b: Inland Waterways Regulations, Rhine Navigation Police Regulations.
options.c: Watercraft Regulation, Water-Skiing Regulation.
options.d: Moselle Navigation Police Regulations, Danube Navigation Police Regulations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-84.explanation: The basic traffic rules for German inland waterways are set out in the Binnenschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung (BinSchStrO); for the Rhine, the Rheinschifffahrtspolizeiverordnung (RheinSchPV) applies additionally/specifically, since the Rhine is separately regulated through the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-85.question: Where can one find the general traffic rules for the Moselle and the Danube?

options.a: Moselle Navigation Police Regulations, Inland Vessel Inspection Ordinance.
options.b: Danube Navigation Police Regulations, Inland Waterways Regulations.
options.c: Moselle Navigation Police Regulations, Danube Navigation Police Regulations.
options.d: Watercraft Regulation, Water-Skiing Regulation.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-85.explanation: The Moselle Navigation Police Regulations (MoSchPV) apply to the Moselle and the Danube Navigation Police Regulations (DonauSchPV) apply to the Danube — each a separate, river-specific set of rules that replaces or supplements the general BinSchStrO for those waterways.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-86.question: Where can one find rules for the operation of personal watercraft (jet skis) and for water-skiing?

options.a: Moselle Navigation Police Regulations, Inland Vessel Inspection Ordinance.
options.b: Watercraft Regulation, Water-Skiing Regulation.
options.c: Inland Waterways Regulations, Rhine Navigation Police Regulations.
options.d: Moselle Navigation Police Regulations, Danube Navigation Police Regulations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-86.explanation: The operation of personal watercraft (jet skis) is governed by the Wassermotorräderverordnung, and water-skiing by the Wasserskiverordnung. Both regulations contain special rules on permitted areas, distances, and conduct that go beyond the general inland navigation rules.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-87.question: What action must be taken if a vessel runs aground within the fairway or navigation channel?

options.a: The vessel remains on site until the water police arrive.
options.b: The water police or the Waterways and Shipping Administration must be informed with exact details of the vessel's data.
options.c: The Waterways and Shipping Administration or the water police must be notified with exact details of the obstruction's location.
options.d: A dredging company must be contacted so the obstruction can be removed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-87.explanation: If a vessel runs aground within the fairway or navigation channel, the Waterways and Shipping Administration or the water police must be notified immediately with the exact location of the obstruction, so that the hazard can be marked or removed for following traffic. There is no obligation to remain on site, and removing the obstruction is a matter for the authorities, not the boater.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-89.question: What is meant by "fairway" (Fahrrinne)?

options.a: It is the part of the waterway whose width is at least 88 m and whose depth is at least 2.50 m.
options.b: The part of the waterway that, according to local conditions, is used by through-going vessel traffic.
options.c: It is the part of the waterway whose width is at least 150 m and whose depth is at least 3.00 m.
options.d: It is the part of the waterway for which certain widths and depths are maintained or targeted for through-going vessel traffic.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-89.explanation: The fairway (Fahrrinne) is the part of the waterway for which certain minimum widths and depths are maintained or targeted for through-going vessel traffic. There are no fixed figures such as 88 m or 150 m, since the dimensions vary depending on the waterway and section.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-90.question: How is shipping informed when certain water levels and flood marks are reached?

options.a: By notices posted at water police stations.
options.b: By nautical information broadcasts (Nautischer Informationsfunk), and announcements on radio, television, and the internet.
options.c: By announcements from the flood control center.
options.d: By notices posted at harbor offices and locks.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-90.explanation: Shipping is informed when certain water levels and flood marks are reached via the nautical information radio service (Nautischer Informationsfunk) as well as announcements on radio, television, and the internet, so that skippers can adjust in good time to changed navigation conditions or navigation bans.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-91.question: Where can a boater determine locally when certain water levels and flood marks have been reached?

options.a: At the notices posted at water police stations.
options.b: At the gauges and marked flood marks.
options.c: At the gauges and the draft marks of vessels.
options.d: At the notices posted at harbor offices and locks.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-91.explanation: On the spot, a boater can read the current water level at the gauges (Pegel) and identify designated flood marks at correspondingly marked points on the bank or on structures, where specific reporting levels can be read directly.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-94.question: In which direction are the banks of a river designated as the right or left bank?

options.a: When traveling upstream, the right bank is on the right.
options.b: From the mouth to the source.
options.c: From the source to the mouth.
options.d: When traveling downstream, the right bank is on the left.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-94.explanation: The designation of a river's banks as right or left is based on looking from the source toward the mouth, i.e., in the direction of flow. This fixed reference is independent of a vessel's actual direction of travel and forms the basis for terms such as upstream (Bergfahrt) and downstream (Talfahrt) travel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-95.question: What does "upstream" or "Bergfahrt" mean on rivers?

options.a: Travel with the current.
options.b: Travel toward the mouth.
options.c: Travel over ground.
options.d: Travel toward the source.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-95.explanation: On rivers, "upstream" (zu Berg / Bergfahrt) means traveling against the current, i.e., toward the source. Its counterpart, downstream travel (Talfahrt), means traveling with the current toward the mouth.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-96.question: What does "upstream" or "Bergfahrt" mean on canals?

options.a: The direction of travel that Part II of the Inland Waterways Regulations defines as "upstream" or "Bergfahrt" for that canal.
options.b: Travel toward the source.
options.c: Travel against the current.
options.d: The direction of travel that Part I of the Inland Waterways Regulations defines as "upstream" or "Bergfahrt" for that canal.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-96.explanation: Canals usually have no significant current, so upstream travel cannot be determined from the direction of flow there. Instead, Part II of the Binnenschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung expressly specifies, for each canal, which direction of travel counts as "upstream" or "Bergfahrt".

sportboot-binnen-elwis-97.question: Which marks bound the fairway on the right bank side?

options.a: Red can buoys or red poles.
options.b: Red conical ("flat-topped") buoys or red poles.
options.c: Green conical buoys or green poles.
options.d: Green can buoys or green poles.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-97.explanation: The fairway is bounded on the right-bank side by red flat-topped (Stumpftonnen) buoys or red poles. This marking shows skippers the lateral limit of the deep, wide water area reserved for through-going traffic.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-98.question: Which marks bound the fairway on the left bank side?

options.a: Red can buoys or red poles.
options.b: Green conical buoys or green poles.
options.c: Green can buoys or green poles.
options.d: Red flat-topped buoys or red poles.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-98.explanation: The fairway is bounded on the left-bank side by green conical (Spitztonnen) buoys or green poles. Together with the red marking on the right-bank side, this forms the uniform buoyage system of inland waterways.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-99.question: Which side of the fairway does a vessel traveling upstream have on its starboard side, and how is it marked?

options.a: The left-hand side of the fairway, marked by green conical buoys or poles.
options.b: The right-hand side of the fairway, marked by red flat-topped buoys or poles.
options.c: The left-hand side of the fairway, marked by red flat-topped buoys or poles.
options.d: The right-hand side of the fairway, marked by green conical buoys or poles.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-99.explanation: A vessel traveling upstream moves against the direction of flow, i.e., from the mouth toward the source; as a result, the geographically left bank lies on its starboard side. This left-hand side of the fairway is marked by green conical buoys or poles.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-109.question: Where does a general prohibition on mooring apply without any special marking of the location or stretch?

options.a: In front of bridges and high-voltage power lines.
options.b: On navigation canals and lock approach channels.
options.c: On navigation canals and in front of lock approach channels.
options.d: In front of bridges and after high-voltage power lines.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-109.explanation: Without any special marking of the stretch, a general prohibition on mooring applies on navigation canals and in lock approach channels, since there is usually little space there, and moored vessels would significantly obstruct through traffic and the approach to and departure from the locks.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-126.question: What does a blue light on a vessel mean?

options.a: The vessel is carrying substances hazardous to health. Keep 50 m distance when stationary.
options.b: The vessel is carrying flammable substances. Keep 10 m distance when stationary.
options.c: A vessel of the supervisory authorities on duty.
options.d: The vessel is carrying explosive substances. Keep 100 m distance when stationary.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-126.explanation: A blue light identifies a vessel carrying flammable substances (dangerous goods marking under ADN). When such a vessel is stationary, a safety distance of at least 10 m must be maintained to keep ignition sources and other traffic away from the hazardous cargo.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-132.question: Which vessel carries the day signal shown below?

options.a: A vessel under 20 m in length, licensed for more than 12 passengers.
options.b: A towed vessel of a towed convoy.
options.c: A vessel aground that cannot be passed on one side.
options.d: A vessel to which the competent authority has granted priority of passage through places where a particular order of passage applies.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-132.explanation: This day signal identifies a vessel to which the competent authority has expressly granted priority of passage at locations where a specific order of transit applies (e.g., narrow canal sections or locks with alternating traffic). Other vessels must respect this priority and allow the vessel to pass.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-133.question: A small vessel under sail is underway at night on an inland waterway and carries a white all-round light at the masthead. What is the practical way to use the white handheld lamp that must be shown when other vessels approach?

options.a: Shine it on the water.
options.b: Shine it on your own sails.
options.c: Shine it on the approaching vessel.
options.d: Hold the lamp pointing upward.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-133.explanation: A small sailing vessel carries a white all-round light at the masthead at night and, in addition, must show a white handheld lamp in good time when other vessels approach. It is practical to shine this lamp on the vessel's own sails, so the approaching vessel can clearly see the sailing vessel's size and position and react in time.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-137.question: When is a pleasure craft no longer considered a "small craft" (Kleinfahrzeug) on inland waterways?

options.a: When it is 18 m or longer.
options.b: When it is 15 m or longer.
options.c: When it is 20 m or longer.
options.d: When it is 10 m or longer.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-137.explanation: A pleasure craft counts as a "small craft" (Kleinfahrzeug) on inland waterways as long as it is under 20 m in length. Once it reaches or exceeds 20 m, it loses that status and becomes subject to the rules applying to larger vessels, for example regarding right of way and marking.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-140.question: How must a sailing vessel on an inland waterway behave when it is on a collision course with a small craft under power?

options.a: It changes course to starboard and reduces speed.
options.b: It maintains course and speed.
options.c: It changes course to starboard and maintains speed.
options.d: It maintains course and reduces speed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-140.explanation: A sailing vessel generally has right of way over a small power-driven craft, since among small craft, vessels under sail are considered less maneuverable and are therefore privileged. As the stand-on vessel, it maintains its course and speed, while the power-driven craft must give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-141.question: How must a vessel carrying a masthead light and sidelights behave toward a small craft with sidelights that is on a collision course with it?

options.a: It changes course to starboard and reduces speed.
options.b: It maintains course and reduces speed.
options.c: It maintains course and speed.
options.d: It must give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-141.explanation: A vessel carrying a masthead light and sidelights is a larger vessel that no longer counts as a small craft. Since small craft must generally give way to such larger vessels, the larger vessel, as the privileged vessel, maintains its course and speed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-142.question: How must a small craft under power behave toward a windsurfer that is on a collision course?

options.a: It maintains course and speed.
options.b: It maintains course and reduces speed.
options.c: It must give way.
options.d: It does not need to give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-142.explanation: A windsurfer counts as a vessel under sail and has right of way over a small craft under power. The power-driven small craft must therefore give way in good time, clearly, and decisively to avoid a collision.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-144.question: What is one of the three basic rules of the Inland Waterways Regulations by which small sailing craft give way to each other?

options.a: If they have the wind from the same side, both vessels must give way.
options.b: If they do not have the wind from the same side, the sailing vessel with the wind from port must give way to the sailing vessel with the wind from starboard.
options.c: If they have the wind from the same side, the leeward vessel must give way to the windward vessel.
options.d: If they do not have the wind from the same side, the sailing vessel with the wind from starboard must give way to the sailing vessel with the wind from port.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-144.explanation: One of the basic rules for sailing vessels giving way to each other states: if they do not have the wind from the same side, the vessel with the wind from port must give way to the vessel with the wind from starboard. This corresponds to the generally known right of way of a vessel sailing on starboard tack.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-155.question: What does this day and night signal mean?

options.a: Floating installation / floating object. Pass at as great a distance as possible, reduce speed, avoid suction and wash.
options.b: Vessel in need of protection. Pass at as great a distance as possible, reduce speed, avoid suction and wash.
options.c: A vessel aground or sunk. Passing on either side permitted at unreduced speed.
options.d: A vessel aground or sunk. Passing not permitted.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-155.explanation: This day and night signal identifies a vessel in need of protection, for example one carrying out work on or in the water. Other vessels must pass at as great a distance as possible, reduce speed, and avoid suction and wash so as not to endanger the people working there.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-159.question: What does one long blast mean?

options.a: Overtaking not possible.
options.b: Engine going astern.
options.c: Attention!
options.d: Vessel unable to maneuver.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-159.explanation: One long blast means "Attention!" and is given, for example, before blind bends, narrow passages, or harbor entrances, to alert other vessels to one's presence in good time.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-160.question: What do four short blasts mean?

options.a: Overtaking not possible.
options.b: Attention!
options.c: Engine going astern.
options.d: Vessel unable to maneuver.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-160.explanation: Four short blasts mean the vessel is unable to maneuver. This warns other traffic that the vessel is currently unable to carry out the prescribed give-way or course-change maneuvers.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-161.question: What do five short blasts mean?

options.a: Vessel unable to maneuver.
options.b: Engine going astern.
options.c: Attention!
options.d: Overtaking not possible.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-161.explanation: Five short blasts mean "overtaking not possible." With this, the vessel being overtaken tells the vessel wishing to overtake that fairway conditions do not allow a safe overtaking maneuver at that point.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-168.question: What is a series of very short blasts?

options.a: A series of at least 6 blasts, each of about a quarter of a second's duration, with a pause of about a quarter of a second between each.
options.b: A series of at least 8 blasts, each of about a quarter of a second's duration, with a pause of about a quarter of a second between each.
options.c: A series of at least 2 blasts, each of about a quarter of a second's duration, with a pause of about a quarter of a second between each.
options.d: A series of at least 4 blasts, each of about a quarter of a second's duration, with a pause of about a quarter of a second between each.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-168.explanation: A series of very short blasts consists of at least 6 blasts, each about a quarter of a second long, with a pause of about a quarter of a second between each. This distinctive pattern clearly distinguishes it from the other standardized sound signals.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-169.question: What does a series of very short blasts mean?

options.a: Vessel unable to maneuver.
options.b: Overtaking not possible.
options.c: Attention!
options.d: Danger of collision.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-169.explanation: A series of very short blasts signals danger of collision. It is given when a vessel recognizes that, despite ongoing maneuvers, a collision is imminent and everyone involved must be immediately urged to take precautionary action.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-173.question: Where can one obtain information about the speed limits in force on inland waterways?

options.a: In the Inland Navigation Licensing Ordinance, from the Waterways and Shipping Administration, and from the water police.
options.b: In the Inland Vessel Inspection Ordinance, from the Waterways and Shipping Administration, and from the water police.
options.c: In the Pleasure Craft Operator Licensing Ordinance, from the Waterways and Shipping Administration, and from the water police.
options.d: In the Inland Waterways Regulations, from the Waterways and Shipping Administration, and from the water police.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-173.explanation: The speed limits in force on inland waterways are set out in the Binnenschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung and can also be requested from the Waterways and Shipping Administration and the water police, since individual stretches may have differing, locally set limits.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-176.question: How must give-way maneuvers be carried out?

options.a: In good time, clearly recognizable, and to port.
options.b: In good time, clearly recognizable, and to starboard.
options.c: In good time, clearly recognizable, and decisively.
options.d: In good time, clearly recognizable, and cautiously.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-176.explanation: Give-way maneuvers must be initiated in good time, be clearly recognizable to other vessels, and be carried out decisively. Unclear, hesitant, or belated maneuvers increase the risk of collision, because the other vessel cannot recognize the intention in time and adjust accordingly.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-177.question: A small craft and a vessel over 20 m in length are approaching on crossing courses, and there is a risk of collision. Who must give way?

options.a: The vessel over 20 m in length must give way.
options.b: The vessel that sees the other on its port side must give way.
options.c: The small craft must give way.
options.d: The vessel that sees the other on its starboard side must give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-177.explanation: Small craft must generally give way to vessels that are not small craft (i.e., over 20 m in length), regardless of the direction from which the vessels approach. The reason is the limited maneuverability and longer stopping distance of the larger vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-178.question: Which vessels underway show only a single white all-round light at night?

options.a: Small power-driven craft under 20 m in length.
options.b: Small power-driven craft and towed vessels.
options.c: Small craft being towed or made fast alongside.
options.d: Vessels being pushed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-178.explanation: Small craft being towed or made fast alongside show only a single white all-round light at night, because as part of a formation they are being carried along by the towing or leading vessel and do not need their own complete set of position lights.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-179.question: How must a small craft under sail, close-hauled, crossing near a bank, behave toward another small craft?

options.a: It must not force another small craft that is keeping close to its own starboard-side bank to give way.
options.b: It must not force another small craft that is leaving its own starboard-side bank to give way.
options.c: It may force another small craft that is leaving its own port-side bank to give way.
options.d: It may force another small craft that is keeping close to its own starboard-side bank to give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-179.explanation: A small sailing craft crossing close-hauled near a bank must respect the bank right-of-way rule: it must not force another small craft that is keeping close to its own starboard-side bank to give way, since that vessel has priority while running along the bank.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-180.question: Who must give way and who does not have to give way?

options.a: The vessel under sail does not have to give way.
options.b: Both vessels must give way.
options.c: The vessel under sail must give way.
options.d: The vessel under power must give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-180.explanation: In this encounter situation, the vessel under sail must give way, because a different priority rule applies here than the usual sail-over-power rule — for instance, a small craft's general duty to give way to a larger vessel.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-181.question: What must the skipper of a small craft observe when meeting vessels that are not small craft?

options.a: Small craft are treated equally to vessels that are not small craft when meeting.
options.b: Small craft do not have to give way to other vessels that are not small craft.
options.c: Small craft must give way to vessels that are not small craft, but do not need to leave any particular room for them to maneuver.
options.d: Small craft must give way to vessels that are not small craft and must leave them the room needed for their course and maneuvering.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-181.explanation: Small craft must generally give way to vessels that are not small craft, and in doing so must leave enough room for these larger vessels to maintain their course and carry out the maneuvers they need, unimpeded. This takes into account the limited maneuverability and greater space requirements of larger vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-184.question: A vessel under sail is crossing an inland waterway. In the middle of the fairway, a small power-driven craft is approaching it, traveling upstream. Who must give way?

options.a: The power-driven vessel.
options.b: The vessel traveling downstream.
options.c: The vessel under sail.
options.d: Both vessels must give way.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-184.explanation: Even though the sailing vessel is crossing the waterway, the basic rule between two small craft still applies: a power-driven vessel must give way to a vessel under sail, since sailing vessels are considered less maneuverable. The oncoming small power-driven craft must therefore give way, even though it is in through-going traffic in the middle of the fairway.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-185.question: Two small sailing vessels A and B are on a collision course (see diagram). Who must give way?

options.a: A must give way. Sailing vessels with the wind on the port side must give way to sailing vessels with the wind on the starboard side.
options.b: A must give way. Sailing vessels with the wind on the starboard side must give way to sailing vessels with the wind on the port side.
options.c: B must give way. Sailing vessels with the wind on the port side must give way to sailing vessels with the wind on the starboard side.
options.d: B must give way. Sailing vessels with the wind on the starboard side must give way to sailing vessels with the wind on the port side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-185.explanation: For two sailing vessels on a collision course, the basic right-of-way rule applies: the vessel with the wind on its port side must give way to the vessel with the wind on its starboard side. Wind from starboard therefore has priority over wind from port, regardless of which boat is currently sailing closer to the wind. This rule corresponds to the internationally recognised give-way rules for sailing vessels and also applies to small sailing craft on inland waterways.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-186.question: Two small vessels under sail are on a collision course. Who must give way?

options.a: A must give way. The windward boat must give way to the leeward boat.
options.b: B must give way. The windward boat must give way to the leeward boat.
options.c: B must give way. The leeward boat must give way to the windward boat.
options.d: A must give way. The leeward boat must give way to the windward boat.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-186.explanation: When both sailboats have the wind on the same side, the position relative to the wind decides: the windward boat (closer to the wind source) must give way to the leeward boat. This is because the leeward boat is more restricted in manoeuvring and course options, while the skipper of the windward boat has a better view of the overall situation. This rule supplements the port/starboard rule for cases where both boats are on the same tack.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-188.question: The lateral distance between boats A, B, and C is constantly decreasing. Which boat may hold its course?

options.a: Boat A, because it is to leeward.
options.b: Boat C, because it is to leeward.
options.c: Boat A, because it is to windward.
options.d: Boat B, because it is to leeward.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-188.explanation: When the lateral distance between several boats keeps decreasing, they are on a collision course. The leeward boat—here boat A—may hold its course, since the other, windward boats must give way to it. The vessel required to stand on must maintain its course and speed so that the give-way manoeuvres of the other vessels remain clear and predictable.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-189.question: Who must hold course towards whom?

options.a: B towards C and A, A towards C.
options.b: A towards B and C, C towards B.
options.c: C towards A and B, B towards A.
options.d: A towards B and C, B towards C.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-189.explanation: In a situation involving several sailboats, the obligation to give way depends on the combination of which side the wind is on (port/starboard) and position relative to the wind (windward/leeward). Boat A, which has the wind from starboard or is to leeward, must hold its course relative to B and C, while B in turn must hold its course relative to C, since C is in the subordinate position (port tack or windward). This staggered ranking ensures that every vessel clearly knows whether it must give way or stand on.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-191.question: A sailboat drifts into the field of a sailing regatta without itself being a participant. Which give-way rules apply?

options.a: Those of the racing rules of sailing.
options.b: Vessels taking part in a regatta must give way to uninvolved vessels.
options.c: Towards regatta participants, the racing rules apply; towards other vessels, the rules of the Inland Waterways Regulations apply.
options.d: Those of the Inland Waterways Regulations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-191.explanation: A sailboat that unintentionally drifts into the field of a sailing regatta without being a participant itself is not part of the race and is therefore not subject to the racing rules of sailing. For this vessel—and equally for the regatta participants in relation to it—the general give-way rules of the Inland Waterways Regulations (BinSchStrO) continue to apply. Regatta participants therefore have no special status towards uninvolved vessels.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-194.question: A small vessel under sail with engine power is beating upstream at night. A vessel is approaching that shows only a single white light. What does this light mean?

options.a: Small vessel without engine power.
options.b: Small vessel with engine power.
options.c: Small vessel under sail.
options.d: Small vessel under sail with engine power.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-194.explanation: Under certain conditions, small vessels on inland waterways may show simplified lighting at night instead of the full set of navigation lights. A single all-round white light identifies a small vessel without engine power—for example, a rowing boat or a pure sailing vessel not running its engine. A skipper seeing this light therefore knows that an approaching vessel has no propulsion and is generally less manoeuvrable.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-209.question: Which technical device against electric shock must absolutely be installed in the shore power supply?

options.a: A residual-current device (RCD/GFCI).
options.b: A surge protector.
options.c: A small charging current is harmless.
options.d: A protective extra-low voltage switch.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-209.explanation: When a sportboat is connected to shore power, there is a risk of dangerous electric shock, particularly due to moisture on board. To protect against this, a residual-current device (RCD, also known as an FI-switch/GFCI) is mandatory, as it immediately interrupts the circuit in the event of a fault current. This is a fundamental electrical safety standard for the onboard installation.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-214.question: To whom may the skipper hand over the helm of a motorised sportboat?

options.a: A person who is at least 18 years old and physically and mentally fit.
options.b: A person who is at least 16 years old and physically and mentally fit.
options.c: A person who is at least 14 years old and physically and mentally fit.
options.d: A person of any age who is physically and mentally fit.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-214.explanation: The skipper is responsible for the conduct of the sportboat and may only hand over the helm to a suitable person. Under the relevant regulations, that person must be at least 16 years old and physically and mentally capable of operating the vessel. Overall responsibility, however, remains with the skipper.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-215.question: How must waste be disposed of?

options.a: No waste of any kind may enter the water; sewage and oils must be disposed of on land.
options.b: Only waste that does not endanger the environment may be discharged into the water 300 m from the shore.
options.c: On lakes no waste may enter the water; on inland waterways special rules apply.
options.d: All vessels must be equipped with sewage tanks and suitable containers for the separate collection of waste on board.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-215.explanation: To protect the waters, a fundamental discharge ban applies: no waste, sewage, or oil of any kind may enter the water. Sewage and oils must instead be properly disposed of on land, for example at designated disposal stations. This rule serves water and environmental protection and applies regardless of the size or type of body of water.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-216.question: What must be observed when repainting the underwater hull or removing the old coating?

options.a: Underwater work may only be carried out by certified specialist companies, in accordance with environmental protection regulations.
options.b: The guidelines of the Ship Survey Commission must be observed for work with underwater coatings.
options.c: The work area must be generously covered, and the resulting waste must be treated and disposed of as hazardous waste.
options.d: Only underwater coatings whose environmental compatibility is indicated by the EU label may be used.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-216.explanation: Work on the underwater hull, such as sanding off or applying antifouling coatings, produces paint and sanding residues that are harmful to the environment. The work area must therefore be generously covered so that nothing enters the ground or water uncontrolled, and the resulting waste must be properly disposed of as hazardous waste. This follows from the general principles of environmental and water protection in boat maintenance.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-218.question: Which side of the fairway does a downstream-bound vessel (Talfahrer) have on its port side?

options.a: The right side of the fairway, marked by red can buoys or floating poles.
options.b: The left side of the fairway, marked by red can buoys or floating poles.
options.c: The left side of the fairway, marked by green conical buoys or floating poles.
options.d: The right side of the fairway, marked by green conical buoys or floating poles.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-218.explanation: On German inland waterways, buoyage is based on the direction of flow, with downstream travel serving as the reference direction. A downstream-bound vessel has the left side of the fairway, marked by green conical buoys or floating poles, on its port side, while the right side is marked with red can buoys. This buoyage system allows skippers to reliably identify the boundaries of the fairway based solely on the shape and colour of the buoys.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-222.question: At what time of day and in what visibility may water skiing be practised on the permitted stretches of water?

options.a: Sunrise to sunset, visibility 1,000 m or more.
options.b: Sunrise to sunset, visibility 1,500 m or more.
options.c: Sunrise to sunset, visibility 300 m or more.
options.d: Sunrise to sunset, visibility 500 m or more.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-222.explanation: Water skiing may only be practised on permitted stretches of water in adequate visibility and daylight. A minimum visibility of 1,000 m is prescribed, along with the period between sunrise and sunset. This restriction ensures that the tow boat, skier, and other water users can recognise each other in time.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-223.question: How must a water skier behave when passing vessels, floating objects, or bathers?

options.a: He must stay on the shore side of the wake.
options.b: He must stay within the wake of the tow boat.
options.c: He may travel up to 10 m outside the wake on either side.
options.d: He may travel up to 5 m outside the wake on either side.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-223.explanation: When passing other vessels, floating objects, or bathers, the water skier must stay within the wake of the tow boat and must not swing out to the side. This maintains the tow boat's lateral safety distance and prevents the skier from getting uncontrollably close to other water users. This rule serves directly to protect the safety of third parties.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-225.question: How must the operator of a personal watercraft (PWC/jet ski) behave outside designated routes or water areas?

options.a: Keep a distance of 10 m from the shore.
options.b: Travel along the edge of the fairway.
options.c: Travel on a clear, straight course.
options.d: Keep a distance of 10 m outside the line of buoys.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-225.explanation: Outside designated routes or areas for personal watercraft, there is a general obligation to travel on a clear, predictable, straight course. This is meant to prevent other water users from being endangered or surprised by tight turns, abrupt changes of direction, or slalom manoeuvres. Because of their high manoeuvrability, personal watercraft are subject to particular behavioural obligations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-227.question: Why must the skipper inform themselves about the applicable regulations before navigating unfamiliar waters?

options.a: Because the applicable regulations always contain important information about bridge clearance heights.
options.b: Because regulations on state waters generally differ in content.
options.c: In order to be able to comply with the applicable regulations.
options.d: Because regulations on federal waters generally differ in content.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-227.explanation: Regulations can differ considerably from one body of water to another, for example regarding speed limits, closure periods, or special rules of conduct. The skipper must inform themselves before entering unfamiliar waters in order to actually be able to comply with the regulations in force there. Not knowing the local rules does not exempt anyone from the responsibility to observe them.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-230.question: Where can extensive information about inland waterways and their boundaries be found?

options.a: In the Inland Vessel Inspection Regulations.
options.b: In Part I of the Inland Waterways Regulations.
options.c: In Part II of the Inland Waterways Regulations.
options.d: In the Small Craft Registration Number Ordinance.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-230.explanation: The Inland Waterways Regulations (BinSchStrO) consist of several parts; Part II contains detailed information on the individual inland waterways, their boundaries, and their particular features. Anyone wanting information about the precise scope, route, or special rules for a specific waterway will find it there. Part I, by contrast, contains the general traffic rules.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-231.question: What must be observed when practising water sports on waters outside federal waterways (e.g. state waterways, municipal and private waters)?

options.a: The permission of the Waterways and Shipping Office must always be obtained, and the respective navigation regulations must be observed.
options.b: The permission of the owner must be obtained where applicable, and the respective navigation regulations must be observed.
options.c: The permission of the owner must always be obtained, and the respective navigation regulations must be observed.
options.d: The permission of the owner must be obtained where applicable, and the Inland Waterways Regulations must be observed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-231.explanation: Waters outside federal waterways, such as state waterways or municipal and private waters, often have their own local navigation regulations (Befahrensordnungen). In addition, it may be necessary to obtain the permission of the respective owner if they restrict access or make it subject to authorisation. This is therefore not an automatic requirement but one that may apply depending on the circumstances.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-233.question: Which authority is responsible for issuing an official registration number for sportboats?

options.a: The German Sailing Association.
options.b: Each Waterways and Shipping Office.
options.c: The German Motor Yacht Association.
options.d: The German Automobile Club (ADAC).

sportboot-binnen-elwis-233.explanation: The state Waterways and Shipping Offices (WSÄ) are responsible for issuing official registration numbers for sportboats. Each office issues registration numbers for its own area of responsibility. This official allocation is distinct from the officially recognised registration numbers issued by private associations.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-235.question: Which bodies are responsible for issuing an officially recognised registration number for sportboats?

options.a: The Waterways and Shipping Offices.
options.b: The water police.
options.c: The German Motor Yacht Association, the German Sailing Association, the German Automobile Club (ADAC).
options.d: District courts that maintain a ship register.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-235.explanation: In addition to the state Waterways and Shipping Offices, certain private associations—the German Motor Yacht Association (DMYV), the German Sailing Association (DSV), and the German Automobile Club (ADAC)—may also issue officially recognised registration numbers for sportboats. These associations have been entrusted by the state with this task and maintain corresponding registers. The registration number has the same legal effect as an official number issued by a Waterways and Shipping Office.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-236.question: When must a watersport vessel be entered in the Inland Vessel Register?

options.a: From 15 cubic metres of water displacement.
options.b: From 10 m of vessel length.
options.c: From 15 m of vessel length.
options.d: From 10 cubic metres of water displacement.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-236.explanation: Sportboats above a certain size must be entered in the Inland Vessel Register, which documents official ownership and legal relationships. The decisive criterion is not length but water displacement: registration is mandatory from 10 cubic metres of water displacement. Smaller boats below this threshold are exempt from the registration requirement.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-238.question: How must a skipper behave when the high-water mark II is reached?

options.a: They must stop the voyage immediately.
options.b: They must observe the navigation ban for vessels without radiotelephone.
options.c: They must observe the ban on shipping at night.
options.d: They must adjust their speed.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-238.explanation: High-water marks indicate water levels at which navigation becomes increasingly dangerous, for example due to stronger currents, reduced bridge clearances, and limited manoeuvrability. When high-water mark II is reached, the highest warning level applies: the skipper must stop the voyage immediately. This is meant to prevent sportboats from being exposed to the significantly increased dangers of flood conditions.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-243.question: What is the meaning of these signs at the marked bridge below?

options.a: Recommended passage with two-way traffic and a lateral limit on the permitted bridge passage.
options.b: Mandatory passage with two-way traffic and a lateral limit on the permitted bridge passage.
options.c: Recommended passage with two-way traffic without a lateral limit on the permitted bridge passage.
options.d: Recommended passage without two-way traffic and with a lateral limit on the permitted bridge passage.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-243.explanation: Signs at bridges indicate how the passage must be navigated. In this case, it is a recommended (not mandatory) passage with two-way traffic, combined with a lateral limit on the permitted width of passage. Skippers must be able to correctly interpret such bridge signals in order to avoid collisions in the confined passage area.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-247.question: Which vessel flies a red pennant at the bow?

options.a: A vessel with priority when locking through.
options.b: A vessel with priority when loading and unloading.
options.c: A vessel carrying explosive substances.
options.d: A vessel carrying flammable substances.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-247.explanation: A red pennant at the bow identifies a vessel with priority when passing through a lock. Other waiting vessels must give way to this vessel when entering the lock chamber. This signal serves the orderly operation of lock traffic, particularly for privileged transports or vessels of the Waterways and Shipping Administration.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-248.question: When is a sportboat considered a small craft (Kleinfahrzeug) on inland waterways?

options.a: When the vessel is 20 m long.
options.b: When the vessel is 25 m long.
options.c: When the vessel is more than 20 m long.
options.d: When the vessel is less than 20 m long.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-248.explanation: The term "small craft" (Kleinfahrzeug) is defined in the Inland Waterways Regulations based on the length of the vessel. A sportboat is considered a small craft when it is less than 20 m in length. This classification matters because small craft are subject in some respects to different right-of-way and conduct rules relative to commercial shipping.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-251.question: Which visual signal may be given at night or in reduced visibility instead of four short blasts?

options.a: Swinging a red light in the upper half-circle.
options.b: Showing a red light.
options.c: Swinging a red light in the lower half-circle.
options.d: Swinging a red light in a full circle.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-251.explanation: The signal of four short blasts is a warning or danger signal indicating an unclear or hazardous situation. At night or in reduced visibility, when sound signals may not be sufficiently perceived, this signal can be replaced or supplemented visually by swinging a red light in the lower half-circle. This preserves the warning effect even when visibility is limited.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-252.question: Which qualification is required to participate in inland shipping radio traffic?

options.a: The CB radiotelephone certificate for inland shipping radio.
options.b: The SRC radiotelephone certificate for inland shipping radio.
options.c: The maritime radio certificate for inland shipping radio.
options.d: The VHF radiotelephone certificate for inland shipping radio.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-252.explanation: Participation in inland shipping radio traffic on VHF radiotelephone equipment requires a specific qualification: the VHF radiotelephone certificate for inland shipping radio (colloquially also called UBI). This certificate differs from the maritime radio certificate (SRC/LRC), since inland shipping radio uses its own channels, procedures, and phraseology. Without this certificate, the corresponding radio equipment on board may not be operated.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-285.question: On a beam reach, how does an over-trimmed mainsail affect the boat's speed?

options.a: The boat stops, because the flow separates from the sail.
options.b: The speed increases, because the wind forces are used more efficiently.
options.c: Heel increases, speed decreases.
options.d: Heel and speed both increase up to a critical point, then drop off rapidly.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-285.explanation: If the mainsail is trimmed too tightly on a beam reach, it is no longer optimally angled to the wind. The angle of attack worsens, reducing forward drive while increasing the heeling component of the wind force. The boat therefore heels more but loses speed, because less of the wind's force is converted into forward propulsion.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-293.question: Why should a well-trimmed sailboat have a slight weather helm?

options.a: Because in an emergency it heads up into the wind on its own.
options.b: Because it is then more demanding to steer.
options.c: Because it then points less well to windward.
options.d: Because it then sails faster on a reach.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-293.explanation: A boat with slight weather helm turns into the wind on its own when helm pressure eases or the tiller is released. This behaviour is an important safety feature: if, for example, the helmsman falls overboard or loses control, the boat rounds up into the wind by itself, loses speed, and does not continue sailing uncontrolled. Good trim therefore provides not only sailing performance but also passive safety.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-297.question: Why is an accidental gybe dangerous?

options.a: It can cause the vessel to lose steerability.
options.b: It can cause injury to the crew, rig damage, and capsizing.
options.c: It can trigger another accidental gybe if the boat does not immediately bear away.
options.d: It can cause a sudden change in the give-way obligation.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-297.explanation: In an accidental gybe, the boom swings uncontrolled and with great force from one side to the other, usually triggered by running downwind with incorrect or missing sail/boom trim. This creates a significant risk of injury to the crew, can damage the rig and rigging, and can cause the boat to heel excessively or even capsize. For this reason, a controlled, announced manoeuvre is required when gybing intentionally.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-92.question: What effects can reaching high-water mark I have for sport shipping?

options.a: Ban on shipping at night and in poor visibility.
options.b: Suspension of shipping.
options.c: Speed restriction and navigation ban for vessels without radiotelephone.
options.d: Overtaking ban and navigation ban for vessels without radiotelephone.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-92.explanation: High-water mark I is the first warning level as water levels rise. Once this mark is reached, restrictions already apply to sport shipping: a speed restriction and a navigation ban for vessels without radiotelephone, since communication with commercial shipping and the waterway authority becomes especially important at elevated water levels. Shipping is only fully suspended once the higher high-water mark II is reached.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-93.question: What are the effects of reaching high-water mark II for sport shipping?

options.a: Overtaking ban and navigation ban for vessels without radiotelephone.
options.b: Ban on shipping at night and in poor visibility.
options.c: Suspension of shipping.
options.d: Speed restriction and navigation ban for vessels without radiotelephone.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-93.explanation: High-water mark II is the higher of the two warning levels and denotes a water level at which the dangers to shipping become so great that navigation must be completely suspended. Causes include strong currents, reduced bridge clearances, and limited manoeuvrability. Mark II is thus clearly distinguished from mark I, at which only speed and radio requirements apply.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-205.question: Which visibility impairments constitute poor/restricted visibility (unsichtiges Wetter)?

options.a: Night, snowfall, heavy rain.
options.b: Fog, snowfall, heavy rain.
options.c: Darkness, fog, snowfall, heavy rain.
options.d: Twilight, fog, snowfall, heavy rain.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-205.explanation: "Poor visibility" (unsichtiges Wetter) refers to weather conditions in which visibility is so severely restricted by phenomena such as fog, snowfall, or heavy rain that safe navigation is no longer possible without special aids such as radar. Darkness or night alone does not count as poor visibility, since sufficient visibility remains possible in clear night conditions with properly functioning navigation lights. What matters is the actual visibility distance, not the time of day.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-206.question: How must a vessel be equipped in order to travel in poor visibility?

options.a: With a fully functional radar system approved for inland shipping and a radiotelephone without ATIS.
options.b: With a fully functional radar system approved for inland shipping and a radiotelephone for maritime radio service.
options.c: With a fully functional radar system approved for inland shipping and a radiotelephone for inland shipping radio.
options.d: With a radar system without a turn indicator and a radiotelephone for inland shipping radio.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-206.explanation: In poor visibility, purely visual navigation is no longer sufficient. A vessel must therefore be equipped with a fully functional radar system approved for inland shipping and with a radiotelephone for inland shipping radio, in order to detect other vessels and coordinate with them. Without this equipment, the voyage may not be continued in poor visibility.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-207.question: What must be observed if poor visibility sets in during the voyage?

options.a: On certain waterways, the voyage must be stopped immediately if radar and radiotelephone are not available.
options.b: On certain waterways, the voyage must be stopped immediately if radar and AIS are not available.
options.c: On all waterways, the voyage must be stopped immediately if radar and ECDIS are not available.
options.d: On all waterways, the voyage must be stopped immediately if radar and radiotelephone are not available.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-207.explanation: If poor visibility suddenly sets in during a voyage, the skipper must check whether the vessel has radar and radiotelephone equipment. On certain designated waterways, the voyage must be stopped immediately without this equipment, since continuing safely cannot be guaranteed without these aids. This obligation does not apply identically on every waterway—it depends on the specific rules for that stretch.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-208.question: What advantage does a radar reflector provide on a sportboot?

options.a: Better detectability of the sportboot on radar screens.
options.b: Better detectability of the sportboot in daylight.
options.c: Better detectability of the sportboot at night.
options.d: Better detectability of the sportboot in poor visibility.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-208.explanation: A radar reflector significantly increases the radar cross-section of a sportboot, since fibreglass and wooden hulls naturally produce poor radar echoes. This makes the sportboot considerably more visible on the radar screens of larger vessels. This is especially important in poor visibility, when commercial shipping navigates by radar alone.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-217.question: What must the skipper of a sailing sportboot on a larger body of water do when a storm warning is issued?

options.a: Put on life jackets. Set sail, try to head for the middle of the water.
options.b: Put on life jackets. Set all sails, try to reach a harbour or a sheltered bay.
options.c: Have life jackets ready. Take down the sails, try to reach a harbour or a sheltered bay.
options.d: Put on life jackets. Take down the sails, try to reach a harbour or a sheltered bay.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-217.explanation: When a storm warning is issued on a larger, open body of water, there is increased danger from high seas and strong gusts. The skipper of a sailboat must therefore put on life jackets (not merely have them ready), take down the sails to reduce the forces acting on the boat, and try to reach a harbour or sheltered bay. Continuing to sail, or even heading for open water, would needlessly expose the boat to the full force of the storm.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-219.question: What weather development can be expected with a rapid and steadily falling air pressure?

options.a: Better weather, rising temperature.
options.b: Bad weather, strong wind or storm.
options.c: Better weather, sunshine.
options.d: Bad weather is not to be expected.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-219.explanation: A rapid and steady fall in air pressure indicates that a low-pressure system is approaching, which is often accompanied by increasing cloud cover, precipitation, and rising wind. The faster and more strongly pressure falls, the more severe the deterioration in weather tends to be—up to strong winds or storms. Falling air pressure is therefore a classic warning sign for water sports enthusiasts.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-220.question: What weather is to be expected when air pressure rises slowly but steadily?

options.a: Better weather, rising temperature.
options.b: Better weather, sunshine.
options.c: Bad weather is not to be expected.
options.d: Bad weather, strong wind or storm.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-220.explanation: A slow but steady rise in air pressure indicates the build-up of a high-pressure system. High-pressure systems are generally associated with calm, largely cloudless, and sunny weather. Rising air pressure is therefore usually a sign of improving weather.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-253.question: What does "radar navigation" (Radarfahrt) mean?

options.a: A daytime voyage using radar.
options.b: A voyage using radar.
options.c: A voyage in poor visibility using radar.
options.d: A night voyage using radar.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-253.explanation: "Radar navigation" refers to a voyage conducted in poor visibility, in which radar is used for navigation and to detect other vessels because visual sighting is no longer sufficient. The term therefore does not simply mean any voyage with radar switched on (for example, in good visibility), but specifically the situation in which radar is necessary to compensate for the lack of visibility.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-271.question: What is the purpose of sail battens?

options.a: To allow the sail to be used even in strong winds.
options.b: To make reefing easier.
options.c: To prevent the sail from luffing/flogging.
options.d: To shape and stiffen the sail.

sportboot-binnen-elwis-271.explanation: Sail battens are narrow strips, usually made of plastic or fibreglass, inserted into pockets along the leech of a sail. They give the sail its desired curved shape (form) and prevent the leech from fluttering or folding over under wind load (stiffening). This produces a more efficient, even sail profile and thus better aerodynamic lift.
